talks.title: Dark Web Digger: Modular Scraping for Dark Web Intel
talks.teaser: Presents a modular scraper that collects dark web forum data to link anonymous accounts to the same user.
talks.summary:
The talk starts with the problem of anonymous users on dark web forums, who keep several aliases and move between sites as forums go offline and return. Tracking which accounts belong to the same person, and which topics are gaining traction, is slow to do by hand. The student presenters, working with a university adviser and a sponsoring cyber insurance company, built a prototype scraper split into independent parts: a collector, a parser, a database layer, and a configuration layer that ties them together.

The collection path runs through the Tor browser behind a VPN, on a Linux server, using Python with Selenium, Beautiful Soup, pandas and MySQL. Logging in still needs a manual step because of captchas, which the team has not been able to automate. Once running, the tool saves forum pages, individual posts and author profiles, writes them to CSV output and a database, and produces per-user files. Config files in TOML let the team swap browsers and target sites without rewriting code. Questions from the audience covered cost, open-sourcing, and whether the approach would hold up against deliberate stylistic disguise.

Next steps involve machine learning: semantic similarity and linguistic profiling to match writing style across aliases, trend detection across users and forums, and a retrieval-augmented chatbot that analysts could query for posts and activity. The presenter stressed that matching would be probabilistic rather than foolproof. The practical takeaways are to design scrapers as swappable modules for volatile sources, and to plan for captcha handling as the main obstacle to full automation.

talks.title: Off The Hook AMA
talks.teaser: Hosts of the long-running hacker radio show Off The Hook answer audience questions about their history, guests and station.
talks.summary:
A panel from Off The Hook, the hacker radio show that has aired on WBAI-FM in New York since 1988, held an open question session at HOPE after one scheduled panelist became ill. The hosts explained that they rarely know the topics until they are on air. They prepare by sharing news articles and listener tips over an email list during the week, and they keep their discussions loose.

The conversation covered the show's history and the people behind it. Panelists recalled studio moves across Manhattan and Brooklyn, and the shift to remote broadcasting after the pandemic, which they built largely themselves. They described memorable guests, including a visit with a former hacker in Pennsylvania, and recalled a 2000 sit-in at the station. During that protest, hosts put a phone on the air while police ordered people to leave, and listeners rallied outside. They also mentioned an April Fools' hoax from 2009 and audio fiction they had produced.

The session closed on preservation. Episodes going back to 1988 are archived on the 2600 website, and the panel argued that recording and keeping community media is worth the effort. Audience members asked whether younger hackers engage with older history. The panel acknowledged that the culture has changed and that bridging generations takes ongoing work, and encouraged listeners to get involved with local radio.

talks.title: The Present and Future of Online Discourse
talks.teaser: Reflects on how well-meant social media and AI tools get weaponized, and what builders can do to steer them.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the speaker's account of building consumer and political technology in the early 2010s, including crowdsourcing and campaign tools. Each project had safety reviews and ethics discussions, yet the same mechanisms were later used for disinformation in ways the team had not anticipated. The speaker presents this as a recurring failure: builders focus on one side of a powerful tool and rarely work through how it could be misused.

The middle of the talk turns to AI and the labor market. The speaker describes tech companies cutting mid-level engineers while keeping senior coaches and low-cost junior staff, and suggests that revenue-per-employee figures are an early signal of where cuts will land. To counter these risks he recommends diverse teams, tabletop exercises that bring in people from outside engineering, failure-mode thinking borrowed from aerospace, and asking whether a system should be built, not only whether it can be. He also argues that verifying humanity may matter more than detecting machine-generated text, and that countering disinformation is hard once facts become political.

In the question period the talk moves to hiring, apprenticeships, teaching students about ethics, and whether online communities can recover from their current state. The speaker's takeaway is that technologists should shape the future they want rather than leave it to others, and that smaller trusted spaces may help people step back from constant online performance.

talks.title: Getting Out of DOGE: A Discussion With a Former DOGE Engineer
talks.teaser: A journalist questions a former DOGE engineer about his time at the VA, contract review work, and the government's software gaps.
talks.summary:
Legal journalist Adam Klasfeld, founder of All Rise News, interviews a former engineer who joined the Department of Government Efficiency in 2025 after years of wanting to ship software for the federal government. The conversation opens with how the engineer was recruited through personal contacts, what a political alignment screening involved, and a first day at the Veterans Affairs central office where nobody was sure what the new hire should be doing.

The middle of the discussion centers on the VA contract review work. The engineer describes a Python script that sorted a very large set of contracts into a shorter list for career contracting officers to examine, stressing that software did not cut anything on its own. They also cover press coverage of that work, a long late-night call with Elon Musk that proved less structured than expected, and an effort to hire in-house developers, which a executive order allowed by redirecting a portion of contract savings to staffing.

In the closing questions from remote viewers and the room, the topics include data access, the overlap with the Government Accountability Office, and the abrupt end of the engineer's access after he answered a press inquiry. The practical takeaways are that federal agencies lack in-house software engineers, that data requests should be justified and logged, and that publishing public-sector code invites useful scrutiny.

talks.title: How a Handful of Location Data Brokers Actively Track Millions, and How to Stop Them
talks.teaser: Explains how a few location data brokers collect and sell device location data, and what individuals and developers can do.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the EFF's examination of a small group of location data brokers that gather precise movement data from millions of phones. The presenters use Gravy Analytics as the central example. A breach exposed records tied to apps ranging from dating and games to weather and finance tools, and many of the app developers involved said they had no idea their users' locations were leaving their software.

The middle of the talk maps two main pipelines. In the first, tracking SDKs embedded in apps, sometimes supplied in return for payment, send location straight to brokers. In the second, real-time bidding in ad auctions lets companies receive coordinates and device identifiers from bid requests even when they never win the ad. The speakers describe how this data reaches government agencies and private investigators, and how it has been used to target people by beliefs, medical visits and other sensitive activity. They argue that the advertising business model rewards collecting as much personal data as possible.

The closing section turns to practical steps. Developers are urged to vet SDKs, request fewer permissions and be open about data practices, while platform makers are asked to offer finer permission controls and better blocking. Lawmakers are urged to pass a federal privacy law with a private right of action. Individuals can reset or delete their advertising ID, audit app permissions, use opt-out services and, in sensitive situations, rely on offline navigation. The speakers reported that data requests they filed with brokers returned nothing about them, which they credited to layered blocking tools.

talks.title: Activism, Hacktivism, and the Law
talks.teaser: Explains how U.S. law treats protest, from pickets and sit-ins to online facilitation and doxing, and where the risks lie.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a disclaimer that the speaker is not offering legal advice and covers only U.S. law as it applies to citizens. The speaker argues that the legal lines around protest should be clear enough that people can tell where they stand, because vague rules discourage participation. The talk then walks through a rough escalation ladder: marches and pickets, sit-ins that occupy space, and direct action that disrupts others, with property damage as the most serious in-person category.

Enforcement tactics get attention, including kettling, pretextual traffic stops, and searches after arrest that can turn a minor offense into a larger case. The speaker suggests clear phrases for declining searches and ending police conversations, telling trusted people your plans, carrying as little as possible, and recording encounters from a safe distance. Online, the talk separates facilitation, such as hosting or payments, from posting and doxing, and explains how computer crime, wiretap, stored communications, and federal doxing laws can apply depending on how data was obtained and shared.

The closing Q&A covers mental health helplines, kettling experiences, the chilling effect of RICO charges in protest cases, and how older or less visible participants can contribute. The main takeaway is to know which category your actions fall into, reduce the evidence you leave behind, and get legal help early.

talks.title: Claw Back Your Data From Big Tech With Cyd
talks.teaser: Shows how the open source Cyd desktop app automates a browser to save and delete social media posts locally.
talks.summary:
The Lockdown Systems collective presents Cyd, an open source desktop app for people who want to recover and control the data they have posted to large platforms. The speakers explain why this matters: old posts can resurface years later, accounts can become professionally awkward, and platforms can restrict access or change terms at any time. Their position is that users should decide where their data lives, how long it stays, and whether it can be moved elsewhere.

The app runs on the user's own computer and signs in through an embedded browser, so the developers never hold account credentials. It scrolls through a profile by injecting JavaScript, and much of the needed data comes from internal API responses that the app captures through a local proxy with its own certificate authority. Deletion sends requests from the logged-in browser context, which is far faster than clicking through each post, and the app backs off when rate limits are hit. The speakers also cover the limits of relying on official archive exports, the cost of reverse engineering sites that change often, and migrating posts to Bluesky with backdated timestamps.

The talk ends with the collective's other projects, OnionShare and a map of ICE detention facilities, followed by audience questions about countermeasures, how often changes break the tool, planned Facebook and Mastodon support, and whether deleted posts are truly gone from company backups. The practical takeaway is that users can keep their data locally, and that contributors are welcome to help add platform support.

talks.title: QWK Packets and the Muffled Spark
talks.teaser: Traces the QWK offline-reader packet of 1980s bulletin boards and the life of its inventor, Mark Herring.
talks.summary:
Jason Scott opens with a primer on bulletin board systems, where a single phone line meant one caller at a time, long waits for busy lines, and expensive calls. He explains how the QWK offline reader, created in 1987 by Mark Herring, solved this by bundling new messages and conference updates into a compressed packet that callers could download and read offline. He walks through the packet's structure, the Sparkware program that produced it, and how the format preserved a large record of BBS-era message traffic.

The middle of the talk turns to Herring himself. Scott recounts interviewing him for the BBS documentary, Herring's later attempt to revisit quick packets, and his death during a swatting incident in which armed police responded to a false emergency call. Scott then explains what swatting is, how inconsistently it is punished across US states, and why repeated federal anti-swatting bills have stalled. He also describes the false calls directed at properties linked to him in January 2025.

Scott closes with practical advice for dangerous police encounters: stay calm, cooperative and still, and let the situation de-escalate. He frames Herring's legacy around the tools and archives that keep early online culture accessible. The question period covers his documentary work, the Internet Archive and manual digitization projects.

talks.title: Hardware Hacking Meets Art: How Movie Special Effects Are Made
talks.teaser: Shows how electronics and prop-building techniques produce practical film vehicles and robot characters that serve a story.
talks.summary:
Davis DeWitt, a filmmaker and former electronics presenter on Mythbusters, argues that practical effects matter because they serve a story, not just because they are technical feats. He starts with a Mythbusters test of whether acceleration can pull a trailer out of sway. The crew needed a full-size remote-controlled Dodge Ram 1500 with a nitrous system, built on a small budget and a short schedule. He used off-the-shelf parts: an Arduino Nano, PWM motor controllers and a radio receiver driving throttle, brakes, a kill switch and nitrous. Failed attempts on the workbench were part of getting it working.

The middle of the talk covers a robot character built for a children's film in about four weeks. Design choices were driven by the story and by the production: soft rounded shapes, worn finishes, a three-wheel base to save power, and a radio link instead of Bluetooth to cope with RF interference on set. Parts were 3D printed so they could be reproduced and replaced quickly, and the team built a duplicate stunt robot with fewer components. He also described a material mistake, using silk PLA with poor layer adhesion, and how the puppeteering and blocking made the character feel alive to young actors.

He closes by arguing that building things that don't make sense widens the set of approaches available for future problems. He also suggests that pivoting after repeated failures is part of the work, and that the value comes from working with ingredients rather than following a recipe.

talks.title: The Quantum Curtain
talks.teaser: Explains export controls on AI, quantum computing and encryption, and how deemed exports limit who may learn restricted technology.
talks.summary:
The speaker, a patent attorney, explains export controls as rules that limit what technology, software, services and knowledge can leave the country. He covers the national security, economic and foreign policy motives behind them, plus civil and criminal penalties for violations. Historical examples include 1990s encryption limits that shaped browser versions, a Japanese review of PlayStation 2 graphics chips, and dual-use items such as life vests.

He then looks at exclusions for published material and fundamental research, and at recent AI model and chip restrictions, some of which were rescinded or changed quickly. Quantum computing is explained through the qubit count and error rate measures used to judge capability. The central concept is the deemed export: sharing controlled technology with a foreign national inside the country can count as an export, so companies need licenses and records before that person can work on restricted projects.

Audience questions covered patent secrecy orders, whether open-sourcing software avoids controls, geographic blocks on cloud access, and whether hosted computing counts as an export. The speaker's takeaway is that these rules are an ongoing balancing act that shifts with technology, so people in affected fields should determine whether their work is proprietary or fundamental research.

talks.title: Tips on Living Life in Interesting Times
talks.teaser: Offers tips for living a good life during turbulent, uncertain times.

talks.title: StickTock.com: An Open-Source Alternative in the Age of Digital Protectionism
talks.teaser: Examines data tariffs and the TikTok ban, and presents StickTock.com, an open-source TikTok frontend hosted in Iceland.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the proposed U.S. TikTok ban, which the speaker frames as a "data tariff" dispute: personal information is treated as a tradable commodity, and restrictions on it can end up favoring large domestic platforms. He argues the bigger problem is the tracking code bundled into everyday apps. He points to tracker SDKs found through static analysis, a large location-data breach, and a demonstration of ultrasonic beacons that pushed advertisements to a phone with its network connection turned off.

The middle of the talk turns to StickTock, a proof-of-concept alternative frontend for TikTok. A user pastes a shared TikTok link, a server in Iceland fetches the video, and the page plays it without trackers, advertisements, or a proprietary app. The service is also reachable as a Tor hidden service. The speaker is candid that it is not a full-featured client, since it depends on TikTok's interfaces and often breaks. A Docker image lets others self-host it, and the speaker described the project's team as stronger on cryptography and communication tools than on web scraping.

The closing message is a call to action: people who care about platform control should help maintain and triage alternative frontends rather than rely on bans or a single jurisdiction. Audience questions covered DeepSeek's network traffic, the risk of narrative control through AI systems, blockchain's effect on privacy, and possible migration paths to federated platforms such as Loops.

talks.title: Hacking the Tech-Industrial Complex: Learning to See Invisible Systems
talks.teaser: Shows how entrenched systems seduce people and how hackers can see and reshape them for the community.
talks.summary:
Seth Godin opens by arguing that the systems around us, from the solar system to modern tech and media, are functional structures people take for granted, and that they tend to protect themselves rather than serve the people inside them. He uses historical examples to make the point: the whaling industry that kerosene displaced, a nineteenth-century recumbent bicycle that racing insiders rejected because it threatened their status, and radio ratings that consultants gamed by pushing listeners to log stations more often. He describes how systems hide behind culture, feel normal, resist challenge, and often treat the user as something other than the customer.

The middle of the talk turns to what to do about this. Godin contrasts hacking for yourself with hacking for a community, citing AIDS activists who followed FDA procedures so closely that the agency had to respond, a chocolate journalist who ended up founding a company, and a Kenyan mobile money service that grew out of a practical use case. He argues that change comes from creating tension, offering a real reason to act, and organizing groups of people rather than working alone. Audience questions covered leadership, cryptocurrency, and how to build a small but committed community.

The closing message is that technology, media, and generational turnover are currently making many systems vulnerable, which he frames as an opening for hackers. He urges attendees to organize, publish their work, and lead by inviting others to join, rather than waiting for permission or relying on fear to motivate people.

talks.title: Ask the EFF
talks.teaser: Takes audience questions to the Electronic Frontier Foundation about digital rights and online privacy.

talks.title: How Law Enforcement Agencies Compromise Entire Encrypted Chat Platforms
talks.teaser: Traces how police compromised criminal encrypted phone networks, from Encom and EncroChat to the ANOM sting and Sky.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a case of cocaine hidden in welding machines shipped to Australia, which were seized after the gang's messages had been read by the FBI. The speaker, a journalist who has covered the encrypted phone industry for about ten years, sets out to explain how such operations work across several investigations, drawing on his book Dark Wire and interviews with sellers, traffickers and investigators.

He describes how handset makers sold stripped-down devices with paid subscriptions and how each platform failed in turn. BlackBerry's shared global key for BBM let authorities read messages, and Encom kept keys on its own server, which allowed Dutch investigators to decrypt traffic. Phantom Secure's operator was pressured into cooperating after an informant lured him, and the FBI then ran ANOM, a supposedly new criminal phone, with a hidden copy of every message. Later, French authorities pushed a malicious update to tens of thousands of EncroChat devices, and Sky was compromised through server-side interception. Each shutdown sent users to the next platform, which the speaker argues law enforcement anticipated.

He closes by noting that ANOM's takedown in 2021 involved hundreds of arrests in a single day, and that smaller platforms have continued the pattern. Criminals have moved toward Signal and GrapheneOS, and he raises concern that these tools could sweep up non-criminal users, citing Telegram's data disclosures. For practitioners, the takeaway is that vendor key management and trust in a provider's architecture matter a great deal for privacy.

talks.title: Not Your Private Army: On the Trail of Cyber Ops
talks.teaser: Traces how states and other interests recruited hacktivists into private cyber armies, focusing on Anonymous and Ukraine.
talks.summary:
Emma Best examines how outside parties have tried to turn hacktivist communities into their own cyber forces. The talk starts with Anonymous, a loose label that anyone could claim, which made it easy for others to use its name. It follows a self-described Anonymous founder who privately acknowledged accepting an offer from Canadian intelligence to work against extremist forums, and it notes a 2008 website attack that was widely blamed on the group but later dropped by the FBI. Other examples include groups that borrowed the Anonymous brand while acting as ransomware affiliates or as state-linked operations.

The middle section turns to Russia after its 2022 invasion of Ukraine. Best describes activists recruited to work with Ukrainian intelligence, with US officials reportedly aware of the coordination. She covers hacks whose impact was exaggerated, a disputed leak tied to a security vendor, and a resistance group whose existence is doubted. Public accounts of who was involved and when, she argues, did not match the evidence she reviewed.

The closing part covers proposals to use hacks to locate military officials, and a sabotage operation in Russia that reportedly caused deaths. Best argues this blurs the line between digital and physical harm and invites retaliation. For practitioners, the takeaway is to scrutinize who sponsors hacktivist claims and to treat state recruitment of activists as a source of compromise and escalation risk.

talks.title: Both Sides of the Wire: Surveillance, Whistleblowing, Building Cyber Peace Movement
talks.teaser: Traces how post-9/11 intelligence practice grew into mass surveillance and urges hackers to pursue a transparent cyber peace movement.
talks.summary:
Former CIA officer John Kiriakou opens with his own experience in counterterrorism after September 11, 2001. He describes how the agency's early hunts in Pakistan relied on improvised, low-technology methods, and how a 2002 capture went badly wrong when the man taken was not the intended target. That account sets up his argument that intelligence work changed quickly once the agency took on a paramilitary role.

The middle of the talk moves to modern surveillance. He draws on the Vault 7 disclosures to describe how intelligence tools can reach cars, televisions and phones, and argues that secrecy around such capabilities leaves the public unable to check them. He also discusses the treatment of whistleblowers, including Edward Snowden, and the gap between legal protections on paper and what happened in practice.

He closes by urging hackers to treat government and vendor tools as a matter for public scrutiny, and to build a cooperative, transparent approach to security rather than one driven by conflict. The question period touched on domestic law enforcement surveillance, classification and the ethics of keeping government secrets.

talks.title: Phrack Magazine #72 - 40th Anniversary Release Party
talks.teaser: Shows how the crew behind Phrack runs an underground hacking zine, from author outreach to physical printing.
talks.summary:
The session, given by the current Phrack editorial team, marks the magazine's 40th anniversary, dating back to 1985. The speakers explain that the new staff took over from the previous editors about two years ago, and that this hardcopy issue is only the second physical release they have produced. Copies were distributed at several conventions, and the speakers describe the logistics of printing and shipping a run of roughly 15,000 copies across continents as the hardest part of the work.

The middle of the talk covers the editorial process. Submissions often arrive as rough drafts or loose files, and a team of editors triages them and works with authors to tighten structure and writing. The speakers estimate that about half of the submissions received made it into the issue, and rejected authors still get detailed feedback. They also note a rising number of AI-generated submissions, which are easier to spot than before. Highlights of the issue include a profile of a notable figure, a hardware-focused paper, and articles that readers can follow at home. A QR-code challenge split across two releases took a week for anyone to solve.

To close, the speakers outline plans for a more consistent schedule, with a summer target for future calls for papers, a website refresh, and more volunteer help, while stressing that frequent physical releases are costly and hard to sustain. The main takeaway is that authors do not need polished prose or a famous name to contribute, and that hacking spans many fields beyond technology.

talks.title: Solving My Identity Crisis
talks.teaser: Proposes DNS-based identity extensions for portable accounts, secure contact exchange, and internet-connected devices with their own names.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the problem that internet accounts belong to the service that issues them, with no practical way to carry an identity from one provider to another. The speaker points to Bluesky, where users attach a DNS name they control to a cryptographic key, and demonstrates signing in with that name to other sites, including a blog and group platform that keeps no account database of its own.

The middle of the talk covers three proposals. The first, called anywhere, extends DNS-handle sign-in beyond the AT Protocol so one identifier works at any site. The second, called anyone, pairs DNS handles with JSContact records so people can publish contact points and encryption keys, with the signing key serving as the lasting identifier rather than the name. Contact data can be passed along through DNS text records, QR codes, business cards or email headers. The third, called anything, describes how a network-connected device could receive its own DNS name, web certificates and an access list of authorized handles, instead of depending on a vendor cloud.

Audience questions covered domain seizure, generating keys with existing libraries, user experience and moving between service providers. The speaker argued that a domain name is only a lookup step and that users can change providers without the old one's permission. The takeaway is a call for implementers to build contact managers, run handle services and help refine the specifications, which are heading toward standardization at the IETF.

talks.title: DIY Police Scanner With SDRs and Open Source Software
talks.teaser: Shows how to build a home P25 police radio scanner from RTL-SDR dongles, Trunk Recorder and Ansible automation.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how US police radio traffic can be monitored independently with a home-built system instead of relying on paid scanners or limited subscription streams. Most agencies use the digital, trunked Project 25 standard, where conversations move between frequencies across talk groups, so a listener has to follow calls as they are reassigned. The speaker explains why commercial options fall short for someone who wants every unencrypted talk group, and why archiving matters.

The described setup uses a home machine with several RTL-SDR dongles running Trunk Recorder to decode and save calls, which then upload to a separate web app, RDIO-Scanner, for live listening and searching recent audio. The manual preparation covers finding the local system and control channel on RadioReference, measuring each dongle's frequency error, and building the talk group list. An Ansible workflow then automates installing and configuring the components. Hardware notes cover a four-dongle, four-core build, CPU and storage use, the effect of sample rate on load, and how a cron job manages archive retention.

The closing section focuses on practical use. Listeners should expect disturbing material, learn the lingo, and remember that radio claims can be false, so information should be corroborated before it is shared. The speaker places the feed within an intelligence cycle and urges advocacy for keeping non-sensitive talk groups unencrypted. The presenter said the playbooks and supporting scripts would be released afterward.

talks.title: When the Lawman Comes Calling: Government Data Demands and Online Platforms
talks.teaser: Explains the legal process behind government requests for user data and how platforms can limit what they disclose.
talks.summary:
The speaker, a lawyer who has handled government data requests at a code hosting company and a healthcare technology firm, starts by laying out the main legal tools investigators use to obtain data from online services. Administrative subpoenas, which need no judge, reach basic subscriber and routing records. A 2703(d) order sits in the middle, carrying a court sign-off and a lower evidentiary bar, and permits ongoing collection. Search warrants reach message content. The talk walks through how courts have stretched decades-old telephone-era wording to cover IP addresses and URLs, drawing the line at whatever a user typed into a request. It also covers national security letters, FISA warrants, gag orders that often accompany them, and how VPN logs can expose users through routing records alone.

The middle section looks at how the law has been tested. Warrant canaries are presented as useful but all-or-nothing signals. The Lavabit shutdown is held up as a cautionary example of ignoring requests and losing credibility in court, while Apple's handling of the San Bernardino case is offered as a model of principled, documented resistance. Jurisdiction through mutual legal assistance treaties and the choice of where data is stored are also discussed.

For practitioners, the closing advice centres on reducing exposure before any request arrives. Keep less data, delete it on a predictable schedule, and move plaintext into users' hands with end-to-end encryption where possible. Respond to overbroad requests with narrowing letters, verify emergency requests, and treat cost reimbursement as a way to deter fishing expeditions. Court challenges are presented as a last resort.

talks.title: Hackers Got Talent
talks.teaser: Hackers at HOPE take the stage in an improvised, good-natured talent show with juggling, songs, magic and jokes.
talks.summary:
Hackers Got Talent is an informal, improvised show held during HOPE 2025. Attendees sign up at the info desk and perform in front of a panel of judges and the audience. Jason Scott, the archivist who hosts the evening, keeps the pace moving as acts are called up one by one, with no script or prepared run order.

The lineup is wide-ranging. Performers juggle, sing a duet, perform a martial arts routine, deliver a rap about decentralized communities, and tell jokes. Others do mind-reading and number tricks, lead the crowd in a wave, or offer on-the-spot hacker names to people who lack one. Several acts are first-time HOPE attendees, and the show leans heavily on crowd participation, with audience singalongs and volunteers pulled onto the stage.

Judging combines the panel and audience votes, and results are announced from the bottom up, ending with a nine-way tie for second place. Prizes are modest and mostly playful: small gift cards from a publisher, a certificate, and a novelty diamond-painting kit for the top act. The main takeaway is the show's spirit. Stepping up and performing, even imperfectly, is the point, and a supportive audience is part of the event.

talks.title: Bureaucracy Hacking - Creating Organizational Exploit Chains for Good
talks.teaser: Explains how to push ideas through large organizations by using policy, stakeholders and bureaucratic process to get things done.
talks.summary:
Adam L. Hesch, a former Navy officer who later worked at Facebook and the Defense Innovation Unit, presents "bureaucracy hacking": finding the weak points in large organizations, which he treats as information systems that store, compute and share information, and using them to create new value. He positions the idea as a response to Pournelle's iron law of bureaucracy, which holds that insiders devoted to the organization itself eventually take control from those devoted to its goals.

The middle of the talk lays out a working framework. It starts with a specific idea and a realistic execution plan, then checks for supporting policy or an approver, builds stakeholder support, ties the pitch to metrics or values, removes friction, chooses a communication style that suits the audience, and identifies the final decision-maker. Hesch illustrates each step with stories: a pitch that eventually led to Amber Alerts on Instagram, pre-staging ammunition on a Navy ship after finding a policy that let a vessel count as underway once its lines were off the pier, a one-word approval for firing signal flares on July 4th, and a drone detection prototype that secured funding through an unspent budget. He also describes winning a slot at an Army mountaineering school by preparing a thorough application folder.

He closes by urging newcomers to frame ideas as serving the organization's goals, to set their own ego aside, to find allies whom leadership trusts, and to look for precedent. In audience questions he applies the same approach to resistant peers and to situations where the decision-maker is hard to reach.

talks.title: Hacking the Future at Tesla Science Center
talks.teaser: Tesla Science Center previews its Wardenclyffe visitor center, ham radio club, space science programs and planned hackerspace.
talks.summary:
The session opens with background on the Tesla Science Center at Wardenclyffe on Long Island, the site of Nikola Tesla's laboratory. The organization has held the property since 2013, and its grounds are not yet open to the public. The presenters explain the center's goal of reshaping science education through hands-on, project-based work, and they link Tesla's wide-ranging inventions, from early remote-controlled devices to radio experiments, to modern technology.

The middle of the talk covers current programs. A space science course for high school students ran last year with 42 participants and is expanding this year to four Saturdays, with units on radio, planetarium visualization, data and an introductory coding workshop. The presenters describe an amateur radio station and club that grew out of an on-air contact, plans for a visitor center with an operating ham station and meeting space, and a proposed hackerspace in a former water treatment plant on the grounds. They also outline a volunteer docent program, community tabling at maker events, and the annual Tesla birthday expo, while noting the funding needs left after a fire at the lab.

The talk closes with a call for volunteers of any background, an invitation to a community picnic and a property visit, and a question-and-answer segment. Answers covered the visitor center timeline and the center's approach to neutral, fact-based messaging amid cuts to museum and library funding. The takeaway for practitioners is a model for building a volunteer community around a historic site through local partnerships and hands-on events.

talks.title: Counter-Surveillance as Activism: Cameras Against State Violence in Israel/Palestine
talks.teaser: Explains how activists in the West Bank use cameras to document settler and military violence, and what happens to the footage.
talks.summary:
The talk defines counter-surveillance as ordinary people monitoring states and corporations instead of being monitored by them. Drawing on three years of fieldwork and interviews with more than 80 people, the speaker focuses on anti-occupation activists in the West Bank who film violence by Israeli settlers and security forces. Most of the cameras are carried by Israeli and international solidarity activists working alongside Palestinians, and they are used both to deter abuses and to record them. The speaker describes the rural context of small farming and herding communities, and how a mobile network of activists moves between villages on shifts.

The middle of the talk looks at what happens to the footage. Activists send it to journalists, rights groups, social media accounts and sometimes courts. The speaker explains that legal geography shapes the outcome: Palestinians live under military law while settlers fall under civilian law, so outsiders face lower risk and their footage carries more weight. Complaints by Palestinians often stall at checkpoints or police stations inside settlements, and conviction rates for settler and soldier violence are very low. The main legal value of the video has been defensive, helping to disprove false charges against Palestinians.

The speaker argues that the impact goes beyond court outcomes. The work builds trust and long-term relationships, changes the views of participants, and keeps a record of events against efforts to erase Palestinian presence. The talk closes with the killing of an activist and the impunity that followed, presenting it as typical rather than exceptional. The audience left with a clear sense of how power, law and footage interact in this setting.

talks.title: The Computer Underground Scene - Past, Present, and Future
talks.teaser: Veteran hackers and phone-phreaking pioneers look back at the underground's past and debate where it goes next.
talks.summary:
The panel opens with each speaker sketching their path into hacking, from 1980s phone phreaking and copy-protection removal to early BBS, IRC and Linux days. They describe a guarded scene where admitting your skills to an employer or family was taboo, and contrast it with today, when companies openly recruit hackers. The talk then traces the move from full disclosure of vulnerabilities to a market for exploits and responsible disclosure.

Later rounds address infighting and doxxing, with speakers arguing that feuds waste energy and that tactics need shared norms. They also cite networked tools that supported activists, from Indymedia coverage of the 2001 G8 protests to the Arab Spring, and compare learning paths then and now, from self-taught IRC and magazine work to hackerspaces, online courses and red-team exercises.

The second half looks ahead. Proposals include crowdfunding legislation, rewarding whistleblowers, mesh radio networks such as Meshtastic and Reticulum that work when connectivity is cut, and smaller invitation-only gatherings. The panel closes by urging that young people be encouraged to explore systems within harmless, reportable limits and that knowledge keep passing through in-person meetings and zines.

talks.title: How to Be Positively Transgressive: Hacking Culture for Good
talks.teaser: Explores how subversive tactics can serve progressive ends, and coins new terms for today's manipulation of culture and attention.
talks.summary:
Johannes Grenzfurthner opens by noting that transgression has been taken up by reactionary movements as well as by artists and hackers. Rather than retelling familiar historical examples, he focuses on language, arguing that the names given to technologies and social patterns shape how people respond to them. He makes the case for a playful but deliberate vocabulary and proposes invented terms for dynamics he sees in the hacker scene and in wider culture.

The middle of the talk works through those terms. They include manufactured dissent, where staged grassroots movements are produced by corporations or political actors, and toxic distrust, where healthy skepticism slides into paranoia. He also covers attention scraping, the harvesting of people's focus by platforms, idolatry politics, irony drift, and the commercial co-option of rebellion as a ready-made kit. He warns that hacker spaces can shrink into hobby clubs. In the question period, he discussed depending on platforms that can remove accounts, the value of running independent mail and web servers, and how to behave around border officials.

He closes with the idea of an empathy payload: subversive acts that carry solidarity and care, not only shock. The practical takeaways are to keep a presence outside any single platform, to pass technical knowledge on to younger people, to stay skeptical without losing grounding, and to ask whether a provocation actually helps anyone.

talks.title: ICEBlock and the Age of Digital Activism
talks.teaser: Explains the design, growth and safeguards of the anonymous ICEBlock app for reporting immigration enforcement sightings.
talks.summary:
Joshua Aaron, creator of the ICEBlock app, explains why he built it after the 2024 election and how it grew to more than a million iOS users within months. He presents it as a crowdsourced early-warning tool: users report sightings of immigration enforcement agents, and nearby users see them on a map. He recounts how press coverage drove rapid growth, and the threats he and his family faced afterward, including the end of his wife's government job, which he ties to the app's publicity.

The middle of the talk covers the design priorities of anonymity, free access and simplicity. He says the database keeps very little: creation and modification timestamps, a packed coordinate value and a deletion flag. Sightings expire after four hours. Safeguards include report rate limits, blocking duplicate sightings, and requiring a real address within a set radius. He also explains why there is no Android version yet, citing push notification design, server costs and the risks of sideloading.

In the question period, he said he will not open-source the codebase for now, and that he has no warrant canary and has received no formal legal demands. Attendees pressed him on false reports, threat modeling, transparency through published design documents or independent audits, and bringing in vetted outside advisers. He said he is open to outside input through his public accounts. The main takeaway for practitioners is the trade-off between data minimization and features, and between secrecy and independent verification.

talks.title: Closing Ceremonies
talks.teaser: Wraps up the 2025 conference with network statistics, thanks to volunteers and hosts, and calls for feedback.
talks.summary:
The closing ceremony opened with thanks to attendees, the audio-visual crew and the volunteer security team, and with reflections on a weekend that ran later in the summer than any previous edition. The network team then gave a recap of the on-site connectivity. They reported about 1,700 devices, visitors from 104 countries, roughly 2.5 terabytes of transfer, and 847 flagged anomalies. The network was monitored but not filtered, and a live dashboard tracked activity during the event. Their findings included a large share of traffic still sent over unencrypted HTTP, several devices beaconing to external destinations, and weak default credentials on some services.

The organizers then covered the supporting work behind the event. They recognized the web and back-end teams, workshop coordinators, and a scholarship program funded by ticket donations. They also thanked the host university's IT and public safety staff, the three-part security model of volunteers, a code of conduct team and campus safety, and the vendors, sponsors and publisher whose support keeps the conference running. A longtime organizer who could not attend in person joined remotely for a short message of thanks.

The session closed with requests for written feedback, recruitment of volunteers for next year, and a call for help with teardown. Speakers encouraged attendees to keep discussing the event and its talks after returning home.

talks.title: Spooky Action at a Discount: DIY Meshtastic Nodes
talks.teaser: Shows how to build low-cost LoRa Meshtastic nodes and how known attacks affect mesh networks.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces Meshtastic, a mesh messaging system that runs over LoRa radio and lets inexpensive nodes exchange encrypted messages, send sensor telemetry, or control hardware across long distances without cell service. The speaker explains the basic building blocks: a LoRa radio chip paired with a microcontroller, often an ESP32-S3 or RP2040, and how those parts shape a node's behavior. Build costs are compared, ranging from a few dollars for bare-bones boards to over a hundred for ruggedized units.

The middle section covers practical setup. Users must pick a region and attach an antenna before transmitting, and modem presets trade range against airtime, which matters in crowded places like conferences. Device roles such as client, client mute and router are compared, with a warning that poorly placed routers can create sinkholes that trap traffic. Encryption tiers are explained: the default public channel is readable by anyone, a shared key protects content while still letting others relay it, and direct messages use per-node keys. Sensors, MQTT bridges and public node maps are also shown, including how shared location can reveal a person's movements.

The talk then walks through attacks seen in research and in the wild. These include spoofed sequence numbers that soft-ban a target node, replayed fake nodes that flood the interface, spoofed node information that changes a victim's name, exhaustion of the limited key storage, and message spoofing on pre-shared-key channels where messages are not signed per user. The takeaway is that Meshtastic traffic is less private than many users assume, and that administrators should harden nodes with remote administration settings and treat shared channels with caution. The speaker closes with the open-sourced Nibble board design and audience questions.

talks.title: A Sleuth's Stories on Detecting and Revealing Large-Scale Research Fraud
talks.teaser: Traces how a volunteer scientific sleuth spots duplicated images and impossible data in published papers across several fields.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with how the speaker, a working scientist, began examining published papers as a side project around 2020. It explains the reporting path: concerns are first posted on PubPeer, then sent to journal editors, whose publishers' integrity teams decide outcomes in a process that can take years.

The middle presents case studies. Reused histology images across treatment groups in Alzheimer's research, including work linked to a senior figure at a major funding institute, appear alongside a rodent vaccine study whose own control data did not support its conclusions. A plastic neck collar study had tables that were identical despite changed labels, and chemistry traces repeated noise across supposedly separate samples. The speaker contrasts simple duplication, found with tools like ImageTwin and Forensically, with subtler patchwork that needs manual matching.

The closing section turns to incentives: high publisher profit margins, paper mills, authorship sold for money, and unpaid peer reviewers. Publishers are described as checking typos more than images. The takeaway is that image screening should happen before publication, and that volunteer sleuths are few compared with the scale of the problem.

talks.title: Hack the Violin Part 2: The Advanced Stuff - This Time There's AI
talks.teaser: Shows how audio analysis and an AI model turned violin recordings into practice feedback drawn from historical treatises.
talks.summary:
The talk follows two violinists who set out to build AI-assisted tools for violin practice. They began with a pitch analyzer adapted from a speech-analysis library, but found its measures, including formants, jitter and shimmer, were designed for the human voice and hard to link to intonation. A rhythm analyzer built on a music audio library came next, but raised its own problems, such as accounting for rubato and aligning multiple recordings for comparison.

The main pivot was timbre analysis using mel-frequency cepstral coefficients, which describe the shape of a sound's spectrum in terms tied to how people perceive it. The presenters recorded the same notes played plainly and then expressively, and an AI chatbot described the difference in descriptive words that matched their own judgement. They then gave the model their teaching notes and several 18th and 19th century violin treatises, which produced practical advice such as singing a phrase before playing it and preparing the sound mentally before bowing.

In closing, the presenters said they had found no other system that turns spectral results into violin coaching advice, and they proposed a future virtual teacher built from master quotations and recordings. In the questions they noted that useful feedback depends on a comparison recording, and that the approach had not yet been tested on double stops or on instruments other than the violin.

talks.title: Into the Fediverse
talks.teaser: Traces how social networks evolved toward the Fediverse, a federated network where users interact across platforms.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a history of computing and networking, moving from mainframes and personal computers through online services, the early web, open source, blogs and RSS. It then shows how social platforms folded the earlier blogosphere into a few large networks. Those networks closed their APIs, relied on advertising and engagement-driven algorithms, and offered data portability that amounted to a one-way download.

The core of the talk explains the Fediverse as a federated system in which independent platforms connect across their boundaries. The speaker, a co-author of the ActivityPub standards, walks through the three parts the W3C settled on: the Activity Streams data format, a client-to-server API, and a server-to-server protocol. He describes uptake by open source software projects and by some commercial companies, along with the difficulties of network effects, portability and encryption for direct messages.

The closing section covers lessons learned. Standards bodies matter, competition between platforms gives smaller networks room to grow, and developers are often easier to reach than whole user bases. Owning a domain was presented as a source of individual control. The question period covered Meta joining the network, alternative protocols such as AT Protocol and Nostr, and efforts to add end-to-end encryption. A practitioner should take away that the open social web depends on implementers and standards work as much as on the platforms themselves.

talks.title: Small Budget, Big Protection: Cyber Defense for SMBs
talks.teaser: Explains budget-friendly ways for small and medium businesses to strengthen security through people, process and low-cost tools.
talks.summary:
Robert Wagner opens with the problem: small and medium businesses often run security with very little money, staff and authority, and tend to repeat mistakes that larger companies made years ago. He frames the gap using the idea of a security poverty line, below which an organization cannot reach basic hygiene, and names money, expertise, capability and influence as the main hurdles.

The middle of the talk focuses on people and process rather than technology alone. He covers hiring a virtual CISO who speaks business language, building a low-cost team of interns and rotating roles so staff teach each other, and writing job posts that avoid biased wording. He also describes free awareness resources, rewards that encourage staff to report odd activity, insider-risk signals that are easier to spot in small companies, and using CIS control implementation groups to set priorities. Risk is presented as probabilities and dollar thresholds rather than heat maps, and assessments are described as more useful when scoped well and run with the testers given a foothold.

Toward the end, he recommends inexpensive technical steps: MFA for everyone including third parties, logging privileged activity, jump boxes as a choke point, immutable cloud backups, regularly reloaded golden images, automation of repeated tasks, and deception tokens such as canary files and honey tables. He closes by suggesting that larger companies and local institutions help smaller ones through advisory boards and shared guidance.

talks.title: Human Augmentation: Hacking Human Perception and Performance With Technology
talks.teaser: Explores how sensory and medical augmentation devices could be attacked, from brain-stimulation research to implant threats.
talks.summary:
Dr. Vimal opens with a survey of the neuroscience behind human augmentation. He moves from invasive methods, such as electrode implants and chemical manipulation of brain circuits, toward less invasive options like cochlear implants, transcranial stimulation, and sensory substitution through the skin or tongue. He explains how the brain's adaptability means almost any sensory input can reshape perception, and describes his NASA-funded work using vibrotactile cues to counter spatial disorientation in simulated weightlessness. He also raises ethical concerns about unregulated neural devices and how stimulation can shift behavior and judgment.

The second half, led by Potter and Palmer, takes an offensive view. They group threats into privacy breaches from passive listening, active interference that changes how a device behaves, and data poisoning that hides an attack's effects. Examples include an insulin pump recall tied to a cybersecurity flaw, location exposure from fitness trackers used near a forward operating base, and scenarios where altered overlays or implant settings could misguide a surgeon or a wearer. Risk is framed at the individual, population, and industry levels.

The talk closes with policy recommendations: open security standards, public security studies for medical devices, closer collaboration between clinicians, regulators, and engineers, and treating medical devices as critical infrastructure. A question-and-answer session follows on open-source design, research collaboration, and the ethics of commercial perception technology.

talks.title: A Red Team Exercise, 15 Years Later
talks.teaser: Shows how Windows EDR products are evaded through AMSI and ETW bypasses, DLL unhooking and process hollowing.
talks.summary:
The talk examines how endpoint detection and response (EDR) products are evaded on Windows. The speaker, a penetration tester and red teamer, contrasts EDR's weighted, telemetry-based scoring with signature-driven antivirus, which he argues cannot keep up with modern attackers. He then explains how scripting engines pass content to the Antimalware Scanning Interface and where kernel-side monitoring sits beneath the Win32 call chain.

The middle of the talk covers bypass techniques: inline patching of AMSI and ETW functions, hardware breakpoint hooking, and provider hijacking against ETW, which the speaker notes is difficult to disable without kernel access. DLL unhooking swaps the hooked copy of a library in memory for a clean one fetched from Microsoft's symbol server, matched by timestamp and image size. The demonstrated chain pairs a PowerShell-hosted .NET downloader with position-independent shellcode that resolves functions by hashed names, then process hollows svchost.exe to run the payload.

The closing points are that effectiveness varies between products and depends on configuration. In the Q&A, the speaker said correctly configured kernel-level telemetry should flag changes to memory protections, while parent process ID spoofing might make an EDR treat a new process as coming from another parent. For defenders, the practical lesson is to confirm that EDR consumes kernel-level events and watches memory permission changes, and to test detections against custom tooling rather than well-known public tools.

talks.title: Eco-Hacking Desire: The Intersection of Pornography, Sex, and Environmental Impact
talks.teaser: Examines how pornography, streaming and AI add to environmental impact, and what greener, more ethical choices look like.
talks.summary:
The talk links sexuality, pornography and sustainability. The speaker, a filmmaker and festival director from Austria, points to the scale of online porn traffic and argues that each viewing carries an energy cost. She sets out fair-production standards, including fair pay, clear consent agreements and transparency about where footage ends up, as a baseline for the industry.

The middle section surveys eco-sexuality, a term linked to Annie Sprinkle and Beth Stephens, and projects ranging from art performances to a fundraising scheme that drew criticism. It reviews greener commercial products and household DIY alternatives, and notes that a few companies dominate adult streaming. Using a study of platform efficiency, it estimates energy use, then covers AI-generated porn, training-data concerns, copyright lawsuits, and public figures on AI emissions and water use, which the speaker said came from outside sources.

The closing argument rejects abstinence in favour of awareness, citing ethical adult sites that compensate performers, fair-trade toys and solar-powered devices. Audience questions covered violent fantasy, AI companionship, advertising, toy waste and piracy, and many were left open for future research. The practical takeaway is that consumer choices, platform transparency and better-made products all shape the footprint.

talks.title: Bitpart: 5-In-1 Platform for Activism Over Signal
talks.teaser: Shows how Bitpart runs one-to-many Signal bots for tiplines, help desks, broadcasts, and eSIM and VPN code distribution.
talks.summary:
Josh King, a developer at Throneless Tech, introduces Bitpart, a Rust-based platform for building one-to-many messaging bots on top of Signal. He traces the project back to an earlier prototype that proved hard to maintain, then describes interviews with activists, journalists and tool builders in eleven countries that shaped the design. Those participants wanted a route to a human operator, explicit consent before anyone is messaged, and no AI posing as a person.

The platform covers five workflows: broadcast lists, anonymous tiplines, a help desk with scripted answers that escalates to an operator, and distribution of prepaid VPN codes and eSIMs. Bot logic is written in a scripting language so contributors need not write Rust. Each bot uses its own Signal account and only replies to people who have contacted it first, which limits spam. Data storage is minimal and encrypted, yet the operator can read message contents. A questioner argued that centrally held identifiers could be exposed through subpoenas to Signal, and that point stayed open.

Other questions covered threat models across very different countries, scaling against Signal's rate limits, and the risk of protocol changes breaking compatibility. Bitpart is AGPLv3 licensed, with a hosted service planned alongside self-hosting on a server or an old laptop. The practical takeaway is to map the threat model and decide who holds which data before building tools for at-risk communities.

talks.title: Data Autonomy: Counter-Surveillance Strategies for Civil Society
talks.teaser: Argues that activists should run their own collectively managed data infrastructure instead of relying only on zero-knowledge apps.
talks.summary:
Marlon Kautz, a grassroots organizer who is facing a prosecution tied to activism, opens with a history of social movements and the state responses to them. He traces the shift from informants and wiretaps in earlier decades to police work built on data platforms, where companies provide law enforcement portals for fast data requests. He argues that zero-knowledge messaging tools, often presented as the answer, have real limits: they face legal pressure and backdoor demands, and they are slow and costly to build and maintain. The organizations behind them can also become political targets.

The alternative he proposes is data autonomy, meaning a movement controls where its data lives, who has physical access to the machines that process it, and how decisions about that data are made. He argues this control should be collective and held by the political groups that depend on it, rather than by a single tech collective that ends up hosting everyone's data. The main obstacle is labor, so he suggests treating deployment and maintenance as code. He demonstrates Co-op Cloud, a set of recipes built on Docker Compose that deploys self-hosted applications such as Nextcloud from a command-line tool, while acknowledging that the work still requires skilled maintainers.

In the question period, audience members raised concerns that self-hosted servers could become identifiable honeypots and that technical power could concentrate in a few people. Kautz acknowledged these trade-offs, including the idea that spreading services across many servers can blur who is connecting to what. The takeaway for practitioners is to treat data infrastructure as core organizing work and to contribute to shared, maintained tooling rather than building one-off solutions.

talks.title: Offworld Voyage: Training for Mars Exploration & Climate Biodevastation on Earth
talks.teaser: Presents zero-waste, plant-based analog habitats for simulated Mars missions and their links to climate adaptation on Earth.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces Offworld Voyage, a decentralized science project that builds ecologically sustainable training habitats for simulated Mars surface missions. The speakers, both alumni of a crew at the Mars Desert Research Station, first explain the field of space analog research and compare several facilities, including Flashline, SAM and Chapea. They frame the project as a way to test ideas that could also help people adapt to climate stress on Earth.

They then walk through the design of the modular M.A.R.S. Tesseract habitats. The planned layout includes a bio-dome for plant, fungi and algae food, a greenhouse for greywater experiments, pedal and solar power, waste recycling, a fabrication lab, a medical bay and living quarters. The crew will wear pressurized suits fitted with biosensors. Planned exercises include simulated illness, time-delayed communication, and mutual aid and consensus decision-making under scarcity. A sound-processing prototype that imitates how sound behaves in Mars's thin carbon dioxide atmosphere was also demonstrated.

The inaugural mission is planned for a remote desert site, with several countries under consideration, and crew applications are open. Results are to be published in analog research journals, and the team is seeking grants and open-source collaborators. The main takeaway is that shared, freely available public science and infrastructure are worth protecting, and the speakers invite others to join the work.

talks.title: rim: Reclaiming Personal Data Sovereignty in the Age of Wearables
talks.teaser: Presents a peer-to-peer model that stores and shares body-worn data across personal devices instead of cloud services.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces rim, a set of protocols and an early proof-of-concept project that aim to keep intimate data from body-worn devices in the hands of the person who generates it, rather than in cloud services. The presenters argue that letting companies collect biometric streams would entrench data extraction business models, so they propose person-to-person storage and sharing. The session opened with hardware demos, including jewelry carrying SD cards and haptic force feedback between two laptops that let collaborators sense each other without words.

The central mechanism, called dissolution, splits data into pieces spread across everyday personal devices so that no single piece reveals anything, and crystallization reassembles it. The presenters described layering Shamir secret sharing over a small key with Reed-Solomon erasure coding over encrypted blocks, so a threshold of pieces is needed to read data while some losses can be tolerated. They suggested that local redundancy could replace remote services such as password recovery, and that a person could keep health or learning records and share them selectively with professionals.

In the questions, the presenters said that someone facing a border seizure could physically destroy the storage on their body, and they suggested separate thresholds for authenticating a recipient and for unlocking data. One attendee asked about using such local storage for health data for people accessing gender-affirming care outside formal channels; the presenters agreed this needed further discussion. The closing message is that building these tools before brain-computer interfaces spread gives policymakers concrete experience to shape humane rules.

talks.title: Aging Cyber Safely
talks.teaser: Examines how scam awareness training and policy can better protect older adults, with findings from a free community workshop program.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the fact that adults over 60 are among the most targeted groups for cybercrime. The presenters cite FBI figures showing more than 100,000 complaints from that age group in 2023, with losses of about $3.2 billion, and Pew survey data showing most people who experienced a scam never told law enforcement. Shame keeps many older victims quiet, which the speakers tie to victim blaming.

The speakers review US legislation from the 1965 Older Americans Act to recent bills on elder fraud and AI-generated voice calls, arguing that little of it pays for on-the-ground education. They point to support lines such as the Identity Theft Resource Center, FINRA's securities helpline and AARP's fraud hotline as key sources of case help. They then describe the Cyber Care Institute, a volunteer-led, free workshop program in New York City that has reached over 100 students through partner organizations. Sessions teach people to pause under pressure, use passphrases, back up data, apply updates and review privacy settings, with added modules on AI and industrial control systems. A small set of paper surveys showed rising confidence, though many participants were unsure how to apply what they learned.

For practitioners, the main takeaways are to replace jargon with plain language, use memorable analogies and games, and encourage participants to bring a buddy so knowledge spreads through their community. The presenters also stress reassurance, since learners often feel the material is too hard, and they plan to refine how they measure results.

talks.title: Hacking Search: Kagi's Revolt Against the Ad-Tech Machine
talks.teaser: Explains how Kagi builds a paid, user-centric search engine that avoids ad-driven incentives and surveillance.
talks.summary:
Vladimir Prelovac, founder of the paid search engine Kagi, begins with his path into computing and his doubts about ad-funded search. He cites Google's own early warnings about advertising conflicts and a 2018 query that showed a sponsored and an organic link to the same site. The core argument is that when users pay directly, incentives shift toward their interests and privacy follows as a byproduct.

The middle covers user-facing features such as blocking or promoting domains, lenses that search subsets of the web, custom URL rewrite rules, and on-demand AI answers. Behind the scenes, a crawler measures how many ads and trackers a page carries as a rough signal of low quality, while results blend several external indexes with Kagi's own and then apply personalization. A small web initiative boosts personal blogs, and a privacy pass built on cryptographic tokens lets users query without the service linking them to an account.

The closing questions touched on international coverage, competition, the cost of paying for upstream indexes, accessibility, and planned profit sharing with publishers whose content feeds AI answers. The main takeaway is that a small team can deliver useful search features without owning a full web index, and that the business model shapes privacy and product choices.

talks.title: No Badge, No Problem
talks.teaser: Traces the history of conference electronic badges and the production and firmware challenges facing a volunteer badge team.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a short history of electronic conference badges, from an early DEF CON design built around a small microcontroller to recent boards based on ESP32-class chips with expansion ports. The speakers explain why badges matter for immersive events and how a chip's documentation makes the hardware approachable for hobbyists.

The middle section covers why this year's volunteer badge run did not happen. Sponsorship commitments fell through, tariffs and geopolitical uncertainty raised costs, and moving the event to an annual schedule shortened production planning to roughly six months. Only a few component donations came through. The speakers outline possible funding routes for future runs, such as badge pre-sales or ticket-price arrangements with the event organizers. The second speaker then walks through firmware options for the badge's ESP32-C3 chip: the Arduino framework, ESP-IDF, ESPHome, WLED and MicroPython. He shows how ESPHome describes hardware in YAML so pin mappings can be reused, and demonstrates personal add-ons such as a display, an infrared controller and a Wi-Fi-connected setup.

The closing takeaway is that the project will keep developing its firmware, is looking for volunteers and sponsors for the next run, and wants to lower the barrier to badge hacking. Documentation, a wiki and a link tree of project resources were shared, and the Q&A covered future puzzles and how the team tests its hardware and software.

talks.title: Systems of Dehumanization: The Digital Frontlines of the War Against Bodily Autonomy
talks.teaser: Maps how surveillance, data brokers and internet laws threaten abortion, sex work and trans rights movements.
talks.summary:
Daly Barnett, a senior staff technologist at the Electronic Frontier Foundation, presents surveillance aimed at abortion access, sex work and trans rights as one connected problem. The talk opens with the historical roots of this monitoring, tracing it back to Victorian-era postal enforcement against obscene material, before moving to present-day threats drawn from privacy and security training with affected organizers, abortion funds and providers.

The middle section covers concrete cases. Location data and license plate reader records have been used in prosecutions tied to abortion, and a company's promised deletion of sensitive location data was later found to be incomplete. Doxing sites repurpose public licensing and business records to target clinicians and activists. For sex workers, the 2018 FOSTA-SESTA laws pushed platforms to over-moderate, removing safety and health resources and pushing people back onto the street, while facial recognition tools were used in arrests. For trans people, the speaker described removed government health pages, school monitoring software that flagged LGBT content, and enforcement schemes that reward informants.

Barnett closes with practical steps: extending protest-style security habits into everyday life, expecting platforms to hand over user data, anticipating harassment, and pushing for comprehensive federal privacy law while opposing age verification mandates. The question round covered prescription drug monitoring programs, censorship circumvention and how activists can answer well-funded opposition messaging.

talks.title: Back to Basics: Building Resilient Cyber Defenses for Multiple Use Cases
talks.teaser: Argues that digital security advice should fit a person's devices, risks and circumstances, and tests popular tips against that standard.
talks.summary:
Yael Grauer, a program manager at Consumer Reports, opens by arguing that digital security advice has changed little even as threats have shifted. She uses gardening analogies, such as attack surface, plant hardiness zones and layered soil, to build a framework for judging whether a recommendation fits a particular person's situation rather than applying it blindly.

The middle of the talk revisits long-standing tips like password managers, multi-factor authentication and keeping software updated, which she considers sound for most people. It then tests newer viral suggestions, including disabling ad IDs, avoiding Signal after rumors about it, using a VPN, leaving phones at protests, changing period tracking apps, and covering cameras or microphones. For each, she weighs the threat model and notes where a tip helps or backfires. For example, pushing someone in a stalking situation to remove stalkerware immediately can increase physical risk. She also points out that some older advice became outdated as the technology changed.

She then describes Security Planner, a free tool that builds a personalized plan from questions about devices and goals, and acknowledges its limits, such as having no support desk. She closes by arguing that individual settings matter less than broader ecosystem change, including legislation, public pressure and holding companies accountable.

talks.title: Zodiac Killer Marketing: Launching a Covert Food Business
talks.teaser: Shows how a vegan food business drew customers through coded billboards, hotlines and puzzles instead of conventional advertising.
talks.summary:
Adam Sobel, a chef whose earlier vegan food truck and restaurants closed during the pandemic, explains why he wanted a smaller food business he could run with his daughter. He rejected hype-driven social media promotion and most point-of-sale technology, preferring handwritten tickets and a personal, hospitable experience where customers talk directly to the cook.

He describes his marketing approach. He photographed poorly designed transit billboards, replaced their text with a custom symbol font, and pasted rewritten versions over the originals. Only a phone number stayed legible. A voicemail gave a decoding key, and the decoded text led to a deliberately misleading website that listed the cart's coordinates. He also mailed printed invitations to the press. Each week's menu changed under a seasonal theme, with most dishes priced between four and eight dollars.

Over time, word of mouth and ordinary discovery replaced the puzzles as the billboards came down, and he stepped back from promotion to focus on cooking. In the question period he discussed the tension between growth and creative control, arguing that scale can separate creators from the people they serve. The main takeaway is that deliberately limiting reach and treating marketing as play can still build a loyal customer base.

talks.title: Leading and Survival When TSHTF - A Lighthearted Look at the End of the World
talks.teaser: Explains how leaders can keep teams steady, safe and motivated during crises, with practical advice on stress and self-care.
talks.summary:
George Sandford opens by framing crisis leadership as relevant to anyone responsible for people, whether as a manager, parent, friend or simply as an individual. Rather than analysing specific real-world events, which the speaker avoids to keep the discussion free of politics, the talk uses a zombie-apocalypse tabletop exercise as a neutral model. The common thread across these scenarios is that human reactions to stress look much the same regardless of the cause, and that the fight, flight, fawn and freeze responses shut down higher thinking.

The middle of the talk draws on research about survivors, arguing that humility, curiosity and adaptability matter more than strength or raw expertise. It contrasts authoritarian leadership, which can work briefly at the start of a crisis, with more adaptive styles needed for recovery, and lists verbal and behavioural markers for spotting safe and unsafe leaders. The speaker also demonstrates a short box-breathing exercise and a nod of connection with the audience to show how quickly people can be steadied.

For practitioners, the closing advice centres on preparation: practise crisis responses in routine work, build psychological safety one-to-one, communicate clearly, look after your own sleep and stress, and let teams take on responsibility. The Q&A adds practical tips on venting in groups, handling adversarial teams, and influencing senior leaders by focusing on measurable impact.

talks.title: The Future of Email Is Open
talks.teaser: Presents OpenEmail, an open pull-based messaging protocol meant to replace spam-prone, surveillance-friendly email.
talks.summary:
The speakers argue that email, roughly fifty years old, was built around a postal model where senders push a message out and lose control of it. They describe how copies pass through several intermediaries, how metadata stays visible even when content is encrypted, and how spam filtering depends on providers reading message contents. They also note that messaging across organizations remains clumsy compared with chat tools used inside a single company.

They then present OpenEmail, an open protocol they call mail over HTTPS, built on a pull model. A sender encrypts a message and uploads it to their own mail agent, then notifies the recipient. The recipient verifies the notice and fetches the content directly from the sender's agent, so it never passes through the recipient's own infrastructure. Contacts pair using hashed addresses so providers cannot see who is talking to whom.
