Public keys are found through profiles tied to email addresses, and the server side is meant to be small enough for a developer to write over a weekend. In the audience questions, the presenters explained that encrypted messages are kept for seven days so that multiple devices can sync, and discussed censorship resistance and whether large providers would adopt the design.

The talk ends as a call for early testers and feedback. The project is still in an early phase, with its code published openly, and the presenters want input before drafting anything formal. The practical takeaway is a set of design choices, such as pull delivery, self-authenticating senders, and client-side handling of edits, offered as a starting point for discussion.

talks.title: Bridging the Decentralized Gap: Hacker Values, Cypherpunk Roots, Blockchains
talks.teaser: Traces the link between hacker and cypherpunk history and Ethereum, covering privacy, open source and the Tornado Cash case.
talks.summary:
This panel argues that blockchain culture grows out of hacker and cypherpunk history. The speakers open with their own paths into hacking and cryptography, recall the first Hope conference in 1994, and describe the BBS and Unix-account culture of that era. They then revisit the fight over the Clipper chip and government key escrow, and the spread of PGP and public key cryptography, as the roots of the push for decentralized and private communication.

The discussion moves to how those ideas show up in Ethereum. One speaker explains a node as a way to run arbitrary software on a replicated ledger, using a failed attempt at a decentralized WikiLeaks as the motivating example. The panelists acknowledge that the 2016 and 2017 token scams left a bad reputation, and they argue that financial privacy matters as much as communication privacy. They cover the Tornado Cash trial and the 2600 DVD source-code case as legal precedent, and survey privacy building blocks such as mixnets, anonymous credentials and zero-knowledge proofs. The Ethereum Name Service is presented as a non-financial public good.

The closing message is a call for hacker and blockchain communities to converge on shared values such as censorship resistance and user sovereignty rather than working in separate lanes. In audience questions, the panel addressed transparency versus privacy on public ledgers, incentive design, and the energy use of proof of work, noting Ethereum's move to proof of stake.

talks.title: Computational Techniques for Making Karaoke Harder
talks.teaser: Shows how a comedy karaoke act rewrites famous songs with fragments from unusual text datasets and the software behind it.
talks.summary:
Robot Karaoke is a live comedy show in which the lyrics of well-known songs are swapped for fragments of text drawn from an unusual catalog of datasets. Jamie Brew explains where that material comes from: copied pages of reviews, competition data published by companies, forum-style questions, government tax forms, wiki articles, a collection of early internet banner ads, and submissions gathered from a community maker space. Each candidate fragment must match the syllable count of the line it replaces, which is worked out with the CMU pronouncing dictionary and extended with manual overrides for missing words.

The middle of the talk traces how the software evolved, from a terminal prototype that needed a keypress for every line, to a browser version with syllable-level timing, a persistent header, and a queue of requested songs. Brew described how the show runs at a regular bar venue and how audience requests come in through a QR code. Several demos followed, including a Blink-182 song rewritten with lines from a federal tax form and a Total Eclipse of the Heart parody built from a hacker film script, with audience members singing some parts.

In the question period, Brew said phrase selection mostly follows existing sentence breaks, with noun-phrase extraction used when sentences are too long to fit a line. Licensing questions led to a plan to open-source the data standard and datasets while keeping song lyrics off public hosting. The takeaway is that noticing and collecting everyday text can be enough to build a usable dataset.

talks.title: Quantum Computing and AppSec: Preparing for the Post-Quantum Threat
talks.teaser: Explains how quantum computing threatens RSA and ECC and outlines first steps for AppSec teams toward post-quantum cryptography.
talks.summary:
This introductory talk explains quantum computing for application security practitioners. The speaker, who has a science background, outlines how qubits differ from classical bits and why superposition and entanglement matter, without going deep into the physics. The talk then reviews encryption, separating symmetric from asymmetric schemes and showing how TLS uses both during a connection setup.

The central argument is that algorithms such as RSA and elliptic curve cryptography depend on problems a large quantum computer could solve, while Grover's search would weaken symmetric ciphers and hashes, making larger key sizes a partial remedy. Harvest-now, decrypt-later collection of sensitive traffic is presented as a current confidentiality risk, and the speaker stresses that timeline estimates keep shifting. The post-quantum section surveys NIST's standardization effort and the main algorithm families, including lattice-based, code-based, multivariate and hash-based schemes.

The closing section turns to practice. Organizations are advised to build a cryptographic inventory, assess which systems hold long-lived sensitive data, and design for crypto agility so algorithms can be swapped with less rework. Hybrid classical plus post-quantum deployment is suggested as a transition path. Challenges raised include larger keys, performance, legacy systems and convincing product teams to act on a distant risk. Audience questions on adoption and trust in standards closed the session.

talks.title: Print, Build, Fly, Heal: 3D-Printed Autonomous Planes in Rural Mexico
talks.teaser: Follows a team building 3D-printed gliding aircraft to carry medicine to remote communities in Sonora, Mexico.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a rural clinic in Sonora, Mexico, where patients in mountainous, isolated communities can be days away from care by mule. A 2014 death, when an antidote could not reach a child stung by a scorpion in time, pushed a local doctor to explore delivering small medical packages by air over roughly 20 km. The speakers explain why quadcopters were ruled out on cost and range, and why a gliding fixed-wing design fit the terrain better.

The middle of the talk traces the aircraft's evolution from an off-the-shelf hobby plane to 3D-printed airframes adapted from an open set of plans. Early attempts brought crashes, a motor that overheated, and lessons about checklists, propeller testing and material choice. Later designs gained larger wings, a phone hotspot for video calls with local health promoters, and autonomous waypoint flights. Local students formed a club, split into operations, logistics and technical teams, and one member trained as a pilot using a simulator and a certification checklist.

The speakers stress that the hardest problem is organizational rather than technical: moving the project from visiting engineers to one owned by local communities. Their plan involves two nonprofit organizations, one in Mexico and one in the United States, and a federated network of university clubs. The talk closes with open questions about cold-chain storage for temperature-sensitive medicines, which they see as a longer-term challenge.

talks.title: Turning Leaks Into Leads With OCCRP Aleph
talks.teaser: Shows how the OCCRP Aleph investigative data platform ingests leaks and registries and turns them into searchable leads.
talks.summary:
This talk from the Organized Crime and Corruption Reporting Project, given by two members of its product and development teams, introduces Aleph, the investigative data platform the group builds for journalists and researchers. The speakers explain that OCCRP operates as a network that supports more than 75 member media outlets, and that its reporters were repeatedly receiving large leaks, registries and court filings with no practical way to search them. Aleph was designed to collect and organize records in advance so they can be queried when a story needs them.

The technical section covers how data is gathered from scrapers and leaks, mapped onto the open Follow the Money ontology, and indexed for search. Records are linked through statements about entities, and properties marked as identifying let new data update existing records rather than create duplicates. Search indexes are tuned for name variants across languages, and lineage is tracked so journalists can see where data came from. A live demo then traced a company tax ID from a breaking news alert about a 2023 bombing in St. Petersburg to a registry record and the owners of the cafe involved, in about a minute. The presenters also showed investigation workspaces, network diagrams, and cross-referencing of a user's own CSV files against the platform's datasets.

Access is granted through a vetted application, with extended data limited to reviewed users and audited regularly. The presenters said a rewrite called ALF Pro is underway, that it will move to closed source with paid tiers for organizations, and that nonprofit journalism will stay free. The main takeaway for practitioners is the value of modeling and indexing messy records before they are needed, and of keeping lineage and identity resolution in the data pipeline.

talks.title: New Journalism: Reimagining Information Networks From the Ground Up
talks.teaser: Argues that community information networks already perform journalism's core functions, and asks technologists to help strengthen them.
talks.summary:
Patrick Boehler opens by arguing that traditional newsrooms have lost relevance because they built their work around large audiences, platform distribution and performative formats, and that funding priorities have often reinforced those habits. Drawing on his experience in exile and dissident media and on research into informal information flows, he points to examples where people already share news outside institutions: crowdsourced tracking of blocked websites and labor protests in China, VPN sharing communities, and checkpoint and road-safety updates in the West Bank.

He then proposes a framework that breaks journalism into roles such as listening, documenting, commenting, inquiring, sense-making, amplifying and navigating, with enabling as the infrastructure layer beneath them. Distribution is only one of these roles. He argues that trust in these networks comes from personal sharing and repeated interaction rather than algorithmic reach, and that the useful question for technologists is which step of the cycle is struggling, not how to push content further.

In the audience questions, he said he had no ready answer on AI-generated noise or on sustainable funding for community-run services, and suggested that institutions may still matter if they are defined by the utility they provide. His closing message to the security audience was to build tools, share what works and help communities own their information networks.

talks.title: NymVPN: The First Real-World Decentralized Noise-Generating Mixnet for Anonymity
talks.teaser: Explains how the NymVPN mixnet hides traffic metadata from global observers and how its two modes compare.
talks.summary:
Harry Halpin argues that a VPN or even Tor still leaves traffic timing and volume visible to a global passive observer, and that commercial VPN operators can read everything they carry. He traces the approach back to David Chaum's mixnet and anonymous credential ideas, which separate who sends a message from its content, and presents NymVPN as a practical version of that work built to resist nation-state surveillance.

The core design combines two ideas. Traffic is split into uniform, encrypted Sphinx packets that pass through several independently run nodes, with each node scrambling the packet so senders cannot be linked to what they send. Desktop clients emit cover traffic so that quiet periods still look busy, while mobile skips this to save battery. A separate fast mode routes packets over the same decentralized nodes using WireGuard across only two hops, trading some anonymity for speed suitable for streaming. Payments use anonymous credentials that are unlinked from the user, and node operators are paid in cryptocurrency, which he acknowledges is controversial.

He closes with the project's status: clients run on major operating systems, the code is open source and audited yearly, and a post-quantum upgrade is underway. He is candid that the software is still buggy and that it does not work well in China yet. The mixnet itself is free to use through Rust, JavaScript, and C and Go bindings, and he invites developers to build privacy-preserving apps on top of it before handing the stage to Lee Felsenstein for a history of technology and social change.

talks.title: Three Revolutions
talks.teaser: Traces the free speech movement, early personal computing and community bulletin boards, and a proposed civic social media design.
talks.summary:
Lee Felsenstein, an engineer who helped shape early personal computing, frames revolutions by mass participation, the overthrow of an existing order, and unexpected consequences. He starts with the 1964 Free Speech Movement at Berkeley, where students sat in, held a police car on campus, and won a faculty vote that ended the university's role as a parent. The organizing through leaflets and a phone room also helped isolated students form a community.

His second revolution is personal computing. A 1973 magazine article on a TV typewriter drew thousands of replies, and the 1975 Altair kit spawned a market for add-on cards. He describes the Homebrew Computer Club sharing software against mainframe norms and resisting IBM's closed designs. His Community Memory project, a free walk-up bulletin board from 1973, showed that ordinary people could use shared terminals. He notes that IBM's later PC had to publish its schematics.

The third revolution, he argues, is reclaiming a communication commons from mass and digital media. He sketches a civic social media system: open source, community-hosted, stewarded by librarians, funded by users rather than advertising, with referrers, journalists, and comment threads that can be answered but never blocked. In the question period he suggested phone numbers as a stopgap for identity and pointed to anonymous mixnet contact discovery as an open project. The design remains unfinished, and he invites engineers to help.

talks.title: The ARTS Open Framework
talks.teaser: Presents an open framework that packages research data, code and figures in containers for reproducible, archived science.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from a common research problem: papers link to data and code, but those pieces are often hard to run or even reach years later, and some government datasets have disappeared from their hosts. Although computational workflows in many fields look alike, from collecting data to analyzing it with code and publishing figures, there is no widely adopted standard for regenerating those analyses across different machines.

The presenter reviewed existing options, including a commercial reproducibility platform, a neuroscience-specific system and an academic project that has gone quiet, and found gaps in openness, scope or upkeep. The proposed framework requires a license and a configuration file, and recommends version control with merge rather than rebase, container files and built images, and trusted RFC 3161 timestamps to prove when data was collected. A demo used a recording of a cheap mechanical watch to show drift analysis, then opened the same environment in a hosted notebook from a shared link.

In the question period, attendees discussed funding mandates and whether overworked researchers will take on extra packaging work. The answer leaned toward setting good examples in well-resourced labs and sharing standard environments, so newcomers can run someone else's analysis without building it themselves.

talks.title: The Political and AI Singularity Are Inevitable - Or Are They?
talks.teaser: Traces how shifts in media shape politics and culture, and how encryption and AI policy proposals fit into that picture.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that politics and culture follow the media environment people live in, and that each major shift from print to radio, television, social media and now AI has changed how people communicate, process information and take part in public life. Drawing on McLuhan's ideas and his four laws of media, the speaker describes a move from book-based, literacy-driven thinking toward fragmented, engagement-driven feeds. The internet, he says, has drifted from an open, decentralised space toward a few centralised platforms whose business model rests on advertising.

The middle section looks at concrete developments. These include pushes for digital identity and passkeys, locked-down Android builds that make custom ROMs harder, AI agents that can read the screen of end-to-end encrypted apps, and the EU chat control proposal. The speaker compares this to the 1990s Clipper chip and warns that AI could make stolen company data easier for attackers to exploit, and that automated decisions could become hard to challenge inside organisations. In the question period, he also argued that large language models are unreliable sources and that truth tends to shift with the medium that carries it.

The closing advice is practical rather than prescriptive. Listeners were encouraged to think about which media they use and how, to favour slower reading and handwriting for deep thinking, to keep trusted identity separate from everyday communication, and to contact representatives about surveillance proposals. The talk ends with a call for media consciousness rather than media literacy, which the speaker frames as a polite label for controlled speech.

talks.title: AI Is Undermining Our Privacy. What Can We Do About It?
talks.teaser: Surveys six ways AI erodes privacy, from opaque data sharing to deepfake misuse, and suggests design guidelines to respond.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a robot vacuum maker found to upload photos, video and audio to train its AI, with consent sought through an app whose promised explanation link did not exist. The speaker treats such gaps as design problems and argues that anyone shaping a user experience is a designer. The talk then sets out six areas where AI erodes privacy: opaque data sharing, accidental exposure, reversal of anonymization, deceptive design, always-on listening, and malicious misuse.

Examples include companion chatbot apps that shared user data with advertisers and offered no way to delete it, a chatbot that leaked personal details when asked to repeat a word, and shared conversations that search engines indexed. The talk argues that anonymized datasets can often be re-identified from a few demographic fields, and that language models can match anonymized text to real people more accurately than humans. It also warns that AI could generate dark patterns, citing a pre-checked recurring donation box, and covers a wearable recorder that kept consent mode off by default and a deepfake video meeting that led to a large fraud loss.

The speaker closes with guidance for designers and developers: make privacy the default, seek explicit consent, disclose clearly what data goes where, warn users before they enter sensitive prompts, collect only justified data, distrust anonymization claims, and offer opt-out and deletion. The talk ends by calling for a federal privacy law and framing privacy as a matter of control rather than secrecy.

talks.title: PrivacySafe and 3NWeb: Engineering User-Centric Digital Sovereignty
talks.teaser: Presents a client-side federation framework that keeps data private and off central servers, with a live demo.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a goal: people want to control the technology they use, trust it, and still find it convenient. Mikalai Birukou contrasts classical federation, like email, where the client tells its own server where each message should go, leaving providers a full record of who talks to whom, with web-style federation. In the latter, a sending client looks up the recipient's service through DNS and connects directly, so communication does not depend on providers cooperating.

Using a two-person messaging example, he shows how messages are encrypted on the device and dropped as opaque blobs into the recipient's inbox, so the server learns neither sender nor content. Recipients confirm senders cryptographically. Encrypted file sync follows the same pattern with randomly named blobs. He admits the first-contact problem has no complete solution, favors physical key exchange, and says the modular design lets other methods plug in. Audience questions covered DNS hijacking and denial-of-service through large junk messages, answered with limited server visibility and size-hinting tricks.

The live PrivacySafe demo covered account creation on a custom domain configured through a DNS text record, password-derived keys that could be swapped for hardware tokens, group chats, separate app containers, and a Linux phone build. The takeaway is that the platform keeps the server side nearly empty of useful data, and app code runs in isolated runtimes, so developers and organizations can build services where users remain in control.

talks.title: Media, Vibe Coding, and the Long Tail
talks.teaser: Explores how vibe coding, revived print magazines and small online communities could reshape media and its long tail of readers.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the speaker's experiment building an AI fact checker in under two hours. A magazine article on fact-checking was fed to an AI model, which drafted a spec, and then a coding platform produced the app. The tool looked polished, but it invented convincing citations that pointed to real websites. The speaker concluded that such tools will not replace human fact checkers soon and that people using language models need their own cognitive guard against plausible output.

The middle section traces media history. An experimental 1960s and 1970s magazine, Aspen, shipped in a box yet kept many print layouts, and a late-1990s magazine, Nest, played with form more boldly. Early web publishing repeated print habits such as banner ads and word-count pay. The speaker also recalled early internet curiosities, including the Trojan Room coffee pot webcam. The long tail idea, that a creator needs about a thousand devoted fans, explains why independent print magazines can sell directly to niche readers at premium prices.

The closing section considers vibe coding for personal and community software, including a social network for reality professionals and a personal CRM idea that venture funding tends to pull toward enterprise. Security was flagged as weak, with the suggestion that obscurity may protect small projects for now. Research on contaminated water after a hurricane showed why small, fast networks matter. The takeaway: media institutions may change more than individual journalists, and trust is built by being trustworthy, while communities can sometimes uncover facts faster than professionals.

talks.title: CRXaminer - Deep Dive Into Chrome Extensions (Plus Tool)
talks.teaser: Explains how Chrome extensions are built and why their permissions are risky, then demos a scanner that rates them.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with why Chrome extensions matter to security teams. Extensions can see and act on every site a user visits, so a single bad one can read cookies or rewrite pages. The speaker walks through real cases: a dark-mode add-on with broad access, a coupon extension that swapped affiliate codes, and a data-loss-prevention extension whose publisher was phished, letting attackers steal business account cookies. He also describes a popular extension bought and redirected without users being notified.

He then explains the file format, a CRX3 that is essentially a zip archive, and the manifest.json that declares granted permissions and target sites. He describes CRXaminer, a Ruby on Rails web app that downloads an extension by its ID, runs rule-based checks, and asks an LLM to adjust the rating using publisher context. Comparing before and after, most critical results moved to high, though severity labels remain hard to make meaningful.

A live demo follows, and the audience discusses cost, prompt design, and whether Chrome's permission model should be more granular. Similar risks were raised for VS Code and Docker Desktop extensions. The takeaway is to scrutinize requested permissions and consider isolating risky extensions in a separate browser profile.

talks.title: Itinerant Signal Institute (Rite of Spring)
talks.teaser: Follows an artist's low-cost air and soil sensing project that links local pollution to climate change and shares readings online.
talks.summary:
Artist Amelia Marzec presents Itinerant Signal Institute, a project that uses inexpensive open source hardware to measure air and soil conditions and connect local pollution to wider climate change. She opens with a weather broadcast she made about a decade ago, then sketches the climate background behind the project: methane released by thawing permafrost, flood risk in New York, and concern that public air-quality monitoring is disappearing.

The middle of the talk covers the build and the field work. Marzec describes a small air sensor for methane and CO2, wired to an Arduino and a Raspberry Pi that sends readings to a project website. Soil samples were collected at sites including Governor's Island, Newtown Creek and locations in Berlin and Poznan, then tested for heavy metals with a soil-testing group. Her main practical problem was networking. Each host site had different restrictions, from locked-down university networks to places with no internet, so she has relied on tunnels and manual uploads. Audience members suggested amateur radio APRS and mesh radio as ways to send small readings without depending on a host network.

The talk ends with the public side of the project, including costumed animal mascots and street performances, and with a discussion of keeping records as the work develops. For practitioners, the useful takeaways are the trade-offs of cheap sensing hardware and the difficulty of deploying devices on networks you do not control.

talks.title: PrivacyTests.org: Web Browser Leak Testing
talks.teaser: Explains how PrivacyTests.org probes web browsers for privacy leaks through systematic leak testing.

talks.title: Packets Over Any Wire: Alternative Networking Mediums for Hackers
talks.teaser: Surveys home networking over coax, powerline and HDMI-over-IP, with security risks and segmentation advice.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that the cabling already inside a house, including telephone wire, coaxial cable and power lines, can carry network packets alongside its original service. The speaker traces the long history of reusing existing wires, from early phone-line links to broadband, and notes that early home wireless and IoT gear repeated the same security mistakes: weak encryption, exposed admin panels and default credentials.

The middle section covers specific technologies. MoCA adapters on coax share one management and data path, ship with identical static addresses, and rely on pre-shared keys that scale poorly, so the speaker recommends point-to-point links where possible. Powerline standards, including HomePlug AV and AV2 and the newer G.hn, are examined for electrical noise, latency and shared-medium collisions. A method is proposed that uses a fully charged UPS to create an isolated setup for provisioning encryption keys. The talk also covers HDMI over IP for whole-home video, synchronised audio through Sonos, radio remotes that work through walls, and how wired ports on wireless devices can accidentally create network loops.

The closing takeaway is to treat each alternate medium as a flat, shared network. Practitioners should segment it with VLANs, such as isolating a garage camera, choose encryption based on how sensitive the data is, and expect older hardware to receive no security patches. Latency and reach should be weighed against the specific environment rather than assuming these links are ready for sensitive use.

talks.title: Aphantasia: A Personal Reflection
talks.teaser: Explores how aphantasia, the inability to form mental images, shapes one pathologist's and teacher's work and thinking.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces aphantasia, the inability to form mental images, and the speaker's experience of living with it. He explains that he assumed people who described "seeing" things in their heads were speaking figuratively until he learned otherwise a few years ago. Drawing on a long career as a pathologist and teacher, he presents the talk as a personal reflection rather than a formal study.

The middle section looks at everyday areas where the condition shows up. He discusses chess, where blindfold play depends on visualizing the board, and piano, where players may memorize scores. He recalls struggling to draw a frog for a school newspaper and finding it hard to describe faces, though he recognizes faces and voices well. He credits pattern recognition and organization as strengths, linking them to reading tissue slides and teaching through analogies, and he asks whether the condition is genetic or more common among pathologists.

The closing part turns to hacking and AI. He proposes that hacking is clever use of technology and recalls writing a backgammon program on a 16K machine during medical school. He suggests that intelligence, imagination and organization may be shared traits among hackers, and he tests chatbots on questions about fictional characters, finding their answers inconsistent. He ends by proposing questionnaires and studies that could explore aphantasia among technical people.

talks.title: Meshtastic Attacktastic
talks.teaser: Examines Meshtastic's LoRa mesh weaknesses in physical access, location privacy and key management, plus a demonstrated device attack.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces Meshtastic, an open-source platform that passes text messages and GPS locations over long-range LoRa radio in the sub-gigahertz ISM bands. It lets groups communicate off-grid without cellular or internet service. The speaker, a longtime security practitioner, found little published security research when the tool spread quickly, so he framed the main risks around physical access, privacy leaks and key management.

On physical access, the small nodes are easy to conceal, and rooftop or grain-silo installations are reachable with basic tools. Defenders can watch for unexpected traffic in the 915 MHz band. Privacy concerns center on GPS position beaconing and route tracking, and one CVE published earlier in the year was cited. For keys, the default primary channel uses weak 8-bit encryption, shared channel keys are passed around by hand without rotation, device randomness is questioned, and remote administration can be enabled by anyone holding the key. The talk then showed a proof of concept built with a community member: a planted radio relayed commands to a Windows machine, which opened applications and typed text.

Recommendations included rotating shared keys, using GPS only when needed, monitoring for rogue nodes with wireless intrusion detection, keeping firmware patched, and blocking unauthorized USB devices. The speaker closed by asking the community to contribute code, review firmware and raise awareness of the risks.

talks.title: Esolangs as a Hacker Folk Art
talks.teaser: Traces esoteric programming languages as a social and aesthetic folk art shaped by hacker culture outside the art world.
talks.summary:
Daniel Temkin argues that esoteric programming languages, or esolangs, should be read as a cultural form rather than dismissed as a category of jokes. He draws on about ten years of interviews with language designers from his blog, esoteric.codes, and on the history of how each language shaped the next. He begins with Dijkstra's essay on the humble programmer, which called for clarity and structure in code. Early esolangs such as FALSE, Brainfuck and Malbolge did the opposite, forcing programmers to show off cleverness within cramped, arbitrary rules.

The middle of the talk moves through several recurring themes. These include elegance, where short programs are admired in a way borrowed from mathematics, and multi-coding languages like Pete, whose code can also be read as an image. Other examples are poetry-based languages that follow Shakespeare-style or stylistic constraints, languages that replace English keywords with Arabic, Yoruba or classical Chinese, and accidental systems such as JSFuck and Turing-complete games and instruction sets that nobody designed as languages at all.

Temkin closes by describing esolangs as a collaborative, community-driven art of constraints, often started by young programmers, and as a counterweight to the push toward AI-assisted code that hides how programs work. He notes that the work is hard to sell, which keeps it outside the art market, and that its open exchange between designers and programmers is what he values most. The takeaway is that aesthetic vocabulary drawn from how programmers themselves think about code fits this work better than art-world terms.

talks.title: Off-Grid Data Running in Oppressive Regimes: The Pirate Box Project (& Sneakernet!)
talks.teaser: Explains how offline Pirate Box networks and sneakernet file sharing can move information past censorship and internet gatekeepers.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that online information is becoming easier to monitor, remove, and gate. The speaker points to book bans, cuts to public broadcasters, and takedowns by registrars and hosting providers as examples. As a counterweight, the speaker presents the Pirate Box, a portable, off-grid mesh-networked file server that visitors join through a captive portal to download or leave files. Hardware can range from a repurposed laptop or Raspberry Pi to a small USB stick with Wi-Fi and a micro SD card.

Much of the middle covers practical setup. Software options mentioned include YunoHost, which can run on x86, ARM, or RISC-V and hosts services such as Calibre, Jellyfin, and Nextcloud, and Copyparty, a Python file server suited to sharing audio. The speaker also describes Project Bookmark, an ESP32-based device for taking and leaving documents, and Kiwix, which packages Wikipedia and other wikis for offline reading. Examples of sneakernet in practice include weekly media drives carried around Havana, Kiwix distribution in Bhutan, and a 2009 South African test in which a pigeon carrying a micro SD card beat a slow ADSL link.

The closing argument is that physical copying can keep material reachable when online channels fail, and that the original Pirate Box project, which closed in 2019, is worth reviving as a community effort. The speaker suggests that anyone can help by copying files onto physical media and passing them along.

talks.title: Things You Wish You Knew About Software Testing
talks.teaser: Shows practical unit testing, CI pipelines and surprising edge cases like leap seconds and emoji filenames that break software.
talks.summary:
This talk argues that software testing is widely accepted as important but often done poorly, and it offers concrete techniques for both programmers and non-programmers. The speaker organises the material around what he calls code breakers, which are test inputs likely to expose defects. The first example is a leap second timestamp that network time servers distributed, which caused some systems to reject it. He notes that a time service can smear the extra second over a day instead.

The middle section contrasts a fix-and-hand-off workflow with unit testing, where a bug is captured in a failing test that stays in the repository to catch regressions later. A Python example using pytest shows edge-case inputs such as empty lists, negative numbers, garbage input and None. Other breakers include leap-year logic that fails in 2100, 13-month finance calendars, and emoji filenames that trip up uploads and shell tools. The speaker lists common frameworks for other languages and explains how mocks replace databases and network calls in unit tests, while integration tests use real services.

The closing portion covers automation with CI pipelines in GitLab, Jenkins, GitHub Actions and Azure DevOps, split into stages for testing, building and deploying. Slow scans such as static analysis can run in overnight pipelines. A git pre-commit hook that runs a syntax checker can reject broken commits before they reach the pipeline. The main takeaway is to turn every bug into a test, add edge cases early, and automate the checks.

talks.title: Build a Tech Community in Your Neighborhood, One Hackathon at a Time
talks.teaser: Shows how a neighborhood tech group runs short biweekly hackathons and how others can start one locally.
talks.summary:
The talk covers how a volunteer group in Flushing, Queens, built a local tech community using two-hour mini-hackathons held every two weeks. The speaker explains that earlier formats such as networking nights, happy hours and talks faded quickly, while hands-on building kept people coming back. A typical session opens with introductions, moves into rapid idea generation, forms small groups around the strongest ideas, works for about an hour and a half, then ends with short presentations and informal networking.

After roughly eighteen months, the group reported about 700 Meetup members, a Discord with around 100 people, roughly ten attendees per session, 38 hackathons and about 140 projects. The speaker walked through a three-phase launch roadmap: initialise the group in the first month, add supporting events and volunteer roles over the following few months, then pursue local business and nonprofit partnerships. Templates for agendas, emails, event listings and social posts, along with a voting tool for ideas, are published openly as a manifesto. Venues were found by asking public spaces such as libraries, community centers and a college, with local representatives suggested as useful contacts.

In the question period, the speaker described governance as based on trust, acknowledged that a written code of conduct was still missing, and explained why a single neighborhood makes a practical scope. Meetup drew most new attendees, while social media mainly helped keep existing members engaged. The main takeaway is to start small, expect early failures, and run a first hackathon to get going.

talks.title: Top Ten: Democratic Open Source SDR and Amateur Radio Applications That Matter Today
talks.teaser: Ranks popular open source software-defined radio and ham radio projects by GitHub star velocity and reviews the leaders.
talks.summary:
The talk sets out to identify the most important open source software-defined radio (SDR) and amateur radio projects without relying on the presenter's own bias. Instead, it uses GitHub star counts across several search terms, including SDR, software defined radio, amateur radio and ham radio. The presenter introduces a "velocity" measure that divides a project's stars by its age, which surfaces newer or fast-growing tools that raw totals hide. The method is also explained as a way to spot trends in any open source field.

The middle of the talk walks through the leading projects. These include a logging application forked from an earlier amateur radio logbook, a satellite telemetry toolkit built on GNU Radio, and a low-cost transmitter board designed to pair with a Raspberry Pi. Receiver software such as GQRX and SDR++ is covered, along with Universal Radio Hacker for analysing and replaying radio signals. Hardware projects include an open source handheld transceiver that connects to a phone over USB-C, a cable that adds sound and keying to inexpensive radios, and the HackRF platform with its upcoming Pro revision and portable firmware. The presenter also notes that a project's update pattern and age can mislead star-based rankings.

The closing advice is to vary search terms, avoid judging projects by stars alone, and test these tools on cheap hardware. Attendees are encouraged to meet others in the field, and the presenter points to a related hands-on workshop and an RF village demonstration at the conference.

talks.title: Unearthing Air
talks.teaser: Explores building personal air quality monitors and reading indoor pollution data through household case studies.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the 2023 wildfire smoke season in the eastern United States, when the standard air quality index gave people little they could relate to. The speaker argues that everyday indoor air matters more than occasional smoke events, since people take in tens of thousands of breaths a day and much of that air is indoors, where it can be more polluted than outside.

He explains that particulate matter is often used as a stand-in for many pollutants, and that both particle size and chemical composition shape health effects. He traces how EPA annual fine-particle limits have tightened over the decades. The build section covers a low-cost PM2.5 sensor common in community networks, wired to a microcontroller over serial connections, along with the need to clean the sensor chamber and to calibrate by collocating with reference instruments. In a project with Salt Lake City newsrooms, monitors were placed in homes and residents logged their activities alongside the readings. Findings included an air purifier that lowered particles while closed windows raised carbon dioxide, and an evening routine that produced a regular spike which dropped once the home was ventilated beforehand.

The closing argument is for pairing numbers with personal, qualitative context so people can make sense of their own data, and for comparing indoor readings with outdoor conditions to decide when to open windows. He invites people working in hardware, software, design or policy to contribute to better local monitoring.

talks.title: Design for Neurodiversity: Creating Neuro-Inclusive Spaces
talks.teaser: Explains neurodiversity and offers practical ways for event organizers to design neuro-inclusive spaces and communities.
talks.summary:
Dorothy Howard opens by framing neurodiversity as a way of embracing neurological difference, a paradigm that grew out of the autistic rights and disability justice movements. She argues that accessibility guides mostly follow legal definitions of disability and seldom address neuro-inclusive design, and that stigma, masking and camouflaging keep many people from voicing their needs. She also reviews research on employment inequities for neurodivergent people and on the unsettled terminology used in science and medicine.

The middle of the talk turns to practical design. Howard recommends captioning and optional cameras for virtual meetings, clear accommodation contacts, and photography consent methods that do not rely only on wristbands. She describes low-sensory and calming rooms, staff training on topics such as sensory overload and autistic burnout, and paying disabled and neurodivergent people to help plan events. Other suggestions cover published food details, varied seating, earplugs, breaks between sessions, and feedback channels that ask about access.

The closing discussion covered competing needs, such as a speaker's vocalizations versus someone's sensory sensitivity, and ideas like a quiet room that streams talks. Attendees shared examples from other events. The takeaway is that inclusive design depends on organizers consulting the people affected and building a culture where needs can be raised without being hidden.

talks.title: Invisible Ink of Compression
talks.teaser: Shows how DEFLATE's flexibility can hide data, enable covert channels, and slip past normal decompression checks.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at DEFLATE, the algorithm behind gzip, PNG and HTTP compression, and argues that its format leaves room for behavior a normal compressor would never produce. It opens with a captured HTTP stream where one copy looks ordinary and another carries extra content in unused parts of the encoding. The LZ77 back-reference mechanism is explained with a short sentence example, and edge cases are then tested by hand-crafting bitstreams and decoding them in CyberChef and infgen-style tools.

Several odd results follow. Back-references that reach beyond the available data produce null bytes, which the speaker traces to how gzip copies memory. Huffman tables can carry unused symbols, or be shaped so the compressed data is entirely printable. Other demos include a gzip file that newer versions reject but older ones extract, a self-referencing archive, a boot-sector puzzle, and a PNG variant where pixel values stay the same while the encoding changes.

To counter this, the speaker built a detector called deflate defector that flags anomalies such as unnecessary literal runs, empty blocks, unused Huffman symbols and statistically implausible code lengths. The closing section covers plans to scan for anomalies in the wild and possible browser or web tooling. The takeaway for defenders is that compressed content can hold data that ordinary decompression will not reveal.

talks.title: The Free Software Movement: Where It Came From and What It Means to Me and You
talks.teaser: Traces the free software movement's origins and licensing battles, and argues why user freedom depends on it.
talks.summary:
Craig Topham opens with a brief history of free software: the GNU project's start in the mid-1980s, the Free Software Foundation, GPL version 2 and its copyleft requirement, the LGPL, the pairing of GNU with Linux, the split that produced the term open source, and the later GPL version 3 and AGPL releases. He then describes his own route into the movement, moving from concern about social injustice and disappointing grassroots politics to finding in free software a concrete way to act. He used it to help neighborhood groups set up websites while explaining the difference between free and open source.

The middle of the talk argues that being able to govern one's own computing is a basic right, and that the freedoms to run, study, modify and share software underpin privacy and free expression. He frames the fight as one front in a wider struggle and says that weakened licensing, such as open-source framing, permissive licenses, or extra restrictions added to GPL text, damages the cause. He surveys the Foundation's current work: certifying devices that run fully free software, handling GPL compliance reports, a stewardship effort against altered license texts, licensing advice, directory reviews, and campaigns on right to repair, software patents and digital restrictions.

In the question period he covered AI training and model licensing, the problem of license proliferation, and mobile phones as a major gap for free software. The takeaways for listeners are to adopt and talk about free software, reach out to projects that misuse licenses, and volunteer with the Foundation's programs.

talks.title: Piracy Is the Past, Present, and Future of Streaming
talks.teaser: Presents Alpha 60, a six-year study of peer-to-peer downloads that maps global media audiences beyond official ratings.
talks.summary:
The speakers introduce Alpha 60, a research toolkit that measures BitTorrent peer-to-peer activity for films, television, books, music and some leaked documents. Since 2018 the project has sampled roughly 568 texts and counted over 4 billion downloads, with anonymized results published on GitHub. Their argument is that official ratings and streaming platform metrics miss much of how audiences actually obtain content. They sample torrent metadata at regular intervals and record only IP addresses and timestamps.

Maps and weekly curves show when and where downloads of shows such as Game of Thrones, Stranger Things and Black Panther spike. A Star Wars case study compares The Mandalorian, Andor, Obi-Wan Kenobi, Ahsoka and The Acolyte, finding that Ahsoka and The Acolyte sustained strong interest over time. Top download locations recur across titles, led by Russia, South Korea, and cities such as Moscow, Seoul and Shanghai. The speakers suggest data center density, military installations and fast connections as possible reasons for unexpected hotspots.

In the question period they discuss mobile downloads as a rough proxy for younger viewers, the limits of inferring demographics from IP data, and how they handle takedown requests and law enforcement queries. They report that their download counts correlate closely with box office figures, while they view Nielsen data with suspicion. The takeaway is that peer-to-peer traffic offers a cross-platform signal of global audience demand, with caveats about bias and privacy.

talks.title: Cracking Enigma: A Chronology of Cryptographic Breakthroughs
talks.teaser: Traces how Polish and British codebreakers broke the Enigma cipher, from rotor deduction to the Bombe's logic.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the Enigma's design and its origins as a commercial cipher device before military adoption. The speaker explains how three rotors, a reflector and a plugboard scrambled each keystroke, and why operating habits such as repeated message indicators and routine daily settings gave cryptanalysts footholds.

The middle follows the chronology. Polish mathematicians deduced internal rotor and reflector wirings from intercepted traffic and a commercial unit, then built cyclometers and bombas to recover settings, until German changes in 1937 and 1938 ended that approach. Their work was handed to British and French intelligence in 1939. At Bletchley Park, Turing's team tackled the naval M3 with statistical methods such as Banburismus, worked through bigram tables, and used a crib-driven Bombe that eliminated plugboard candidates through logical contradictions.

The closing audience questions covered German security responses, the limited role of linguists, and how rotor wirings were chosen. The practical takeaway is that the breaks came from procedural weaknesses and statistical reasoning layered over mechanical computation, rather than from one single flaw in the machine.

talks.title: Hacking for Social Justice
talks.teaser: Explains how hackers can align technical skills with social movements, from digital safety to supporting nonprofits.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the question of how hacking skills can serve social justice and argues that many technically skilled people want to help but lack a clear goal. The speaker, who works with nonprofits and grassroots groups, frames justice in concrete terms such as equal rights, fair distribution of resources, and dismantling exploitative structures. A useful starting point, the speaker suggests, is to name who you want to protect, what you want to protect them from, and which support pillars of an unjust system you aim to weaken.

The middle section covers how movements grow. Drawing on research on the roughly 3.5 percent participation threshold, the speaker argues that lone actions such as breaches or defacements fade quickly, while broad participation sustains change. The talk walks through movement phases, from trigger events to escalation, disillusionment and a new normal, and gives examples such as safe documentation, reporting channels, coordinated leaks with journalists, and nonviolent tactics. Accessible tools and plain-language privacy guides are presented as ways to lower barriers for ordinary participants.

The closing section offers an action checklist: define a purpose, engage communities before building tools, protect movements from harassment before a crisis, pace yourself, and seek paid work rather than relying only on volunteers. The audience Q&A touched on debates over tactics, and the speaker noted that many activist groups lack basic digital safety practices and sustainable funding.

talks.title: Communication and Movement in Internet Shutdown Protests: Rethinking Mesh Messaging
talks.teaser: Examines how protesters move during internet shutdowns and why current mesh messaging tools struggle in real crowds.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the scale of internet shutdowns, which reached a record 296 documented events across 54 countries in 2024. The speaker explains that shutdowns cluster around protests, elections and coups, and that they cut off emergency calls and protest coordination. Mesh messaging, which relays messages device to device over short-range links such as Bluetooth or Wi-Fi Direct, is often proposed as a fallback.

The speaker then reviews FireChat and Bridgefy, two mesh apps widely used during protests in Hong Kong. Both were designed for festivals and crowded venues rather than demonstrations. Security analyses found unencrypted local storage, weak authenticity and tracking risks, and later research showed that Bridgefy's Signal-based fix was implemented incorrectly and could still be attacked. Simulation studies usually rely on random waypoint mobility models, which ignore how crowds actually behave: people match the pace of nearby companions, travel in bonded pairs, channel along buildings and scatter when confronted.

Based on a review of public footage, the research plans interviews with demonstrators, organizers and journalists to build more realistic movement models and then evaluate mesh schemes against them. Participants can withdraw their testimony at any point, and the speaker notes that such models could also be misused by repressive actors. The practical takeaway is that mesh tools for protests should be tested against realistic human movement before deployment.

talks.title: Expanding BioArtBot Color Palette - A Beginner's Guide to Lab Automation & Biosafety
talks.teaser: Shows how an open-source pipetting robot paints pixel art with colored bacteria, and how new pigments were found and checked.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces BioArtBot, a web-driven art project in which users submit pixel art and an open-source OT2 pipetting robot deposits colored bacteria onto agar. The speaker, a microbiologist who helps run a volunteer community biology lab in New York City, presents it as an entry point into lab automation and synthetic biology, and contrasts it with the scarcity of beginner-friendly biology platforms compared with electronics kits.

The middle of the talk covers the work of expanding the color palette. Rather than relying only on engineered strains, the team sourced natural pigments in two ways: isolating a mold found in home compost, and requesting environmental organisms, such as microbes from solar panels, that were described in published papers. Identification used commercial protein and DNA services, and DNA matching succeeded where the protein method did not. Practical problems included a colony that spread across the whole plate instead of forming single pixels, which was addressed by changing the growth medium. Unidentified organisms were handled under biosafety cabinets until their risk group was known.

The closing section argues that organisms should be identified and assigned a risk group before they are shared or grown in open spaces. The speaker points to the codebase as a framework for contributors, for example by adding new brush styles or sourcing new pigments. Audience questions covered running the web app locally, how long colonies last, and whether a still air box could replace a fume hood.

talks.title: RDP Spray and Pray: Research on Modern RDP Attacks From Spray to Exploit
talks.teaser: Surveys modern RDP attacks against MFA-enabled systems and shows how spray and fatigue patterns appear in authentication logs.
talks.summary:
Tess Mishoe, an AI security researcher and engineer on Cisco's Duo team, traces Remote Desktop Protocol from its 1998 debut through BlueKeep and the later addition of MFA. She explains the common attack paths: credential brute forcing with common tools, exploiting old vulnerabilities, lateral movement using stolen access, and denial of service that can trigger fail-open conditions when MFA breaks down.

The middle of the talk turns to authentication data from a large set of MFA-protected RDP environments. Mishoe describes broad spray campaigns that cycle through users to avoid lockouts, MFA fatigue through repeated push prompts, and quiet single-account attempts that succeed because of leftover bypass settings. She reviews where attempts originate, which industries are hit hardest, such as manufacturing and IT services, and how her team labels traffic to train a detection model, with human review at each step.

She closes with practical defenses: keep RDP off the open internet, keep MFA enabled despite its limits, audit permissions and bypass rules regularly, and tighten conditional access and device enrollment. Her main point is that automation helps detection, but analysts are still needed to recognize new patterns.

talks.title: The Trials and Tribulations of Building Your Own Phone
talks.teaser: Follows one hobbyist's effort to design an open source phone with privacy and intentional disconnection in mind.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the case for building a phone rather than buying one. The speaker argues that smartphones and mobile networks expose location, contacts, and browsing data, pointing to SS7 weaknesses, cell-site simulators, data brokers, and ad-tech tracking. Privacy and a wish to step back from constant connectivity drove the project, which the speaker presents as an unfinished journey rather than a guide.

The modem came first. Datasheets sat behind registration forms, and one sales contact claimed carrier certification was required, though it never was. The speaker settled on a SIM7600 module over a certified system-on-module. A first custom breakout board with antenna connectors, a SIM slot, audio, and level shifters did not power on, so a Raspberry Pi hat was used in the meantime. The software layer was a Rust service that talked to the modem over serial using the Hayes command set, until the speaker found that ModemManager already handled that work. Planned features include a standalone Linux device, Signal-based messaging, encryption of data at rest, hardware switches to cut power to the modem and microphone, and stingray detection.

The project remains early, with no formal contribution channels yet. The speaker plans to post updates and slides on a personal site and invites feedback. For practitioners, the talk shows that RF board work is more approachable when vendor reference designs are followed, and that existing system services should be checked before writing new ones. Open questions raised in Q&A include whether silent SMS could be detected, how to handle battery life, and which form factor to pursue.

talks.title: ATM Hacking: Past and Present
talks.teaser: Traces ATM cash-out attacks from magstripe skimming to a coin dispenser flusher built from a bought unit.
talks.summary:
The talk traces how ATM attacks have changed over time, starting with embossed cards and magnetic stripes. It explains how track two data is structured, why the discretionary field once protected card data, and how weak implementations allowed criminals to build valid track data without the bank's cryptographic material. Skimmers and the shift from physical data capture to online fraud are also covered.

The focus then moves to ATM internals. The speaker describes how exposed USB ports on some machines can give an attacker a route out of the vendor interface to the operating system, and how cash dispensers connected over USB can be commanded by specialised software that criminal markets sell. To make this concrete, the speaker takes a low-cost coin dispenser bought online without any software, captures its USB traffic with a sniffer, and uses an LLM to help interpret the request and response blocks into a working proof of concept.

The talk ends with a live demo of a standalone black box device that runs in USB host mode and triggers coin dispensing without a host computer, with Wi-Fi control discussed as a possibility. The takeaways point to checking exposed ports, not assuming vendor software is secure, and treating cash-handling hardware as an embedded target. The Q&A touched on quantum threats, contactless access and the role of the magnetic stripe today.

talks.title: Exploiting Emergent Property-Based Vulnerabilities in Large Language Models
talks.teaser: Presents jailbreak and context-manipulation attacks that bypass LLM guardrails, and explains why these emergent flaws persist.
talks.summary:
The talk begins with the idea that emergent behavior appears when complex systems interact, and that it is hard to predict without scaling them up. The speaker applies this to large language models, which are usually wrapped in a middle layer of filters, retrieval components and prompt assembly. Attacks that get past that layer can reach the core model more directly.

Several techniques are demonstrated. One anchors the model to an earlier year so that its guardrails respond differently. Another stacks nested fictional contexts until the model loses track of its constraints. A third uses poetic phrasing in a non-English prompt to coax out content it should withhold. The speaker reports that some of these worked across many commercial and open models. He also covers a roleplay attack against a voice-driven game character that exploited contradictory instructions and a small context window, and persistent tuning keywords that altered chat behavior.

Disclosure to AI vendors was often unproductive, according to the speaker, who argues that the middle layer should be transparent and auditable. The main takeaway is to test these systems hands-on, observe how responses shift with wording, and document the results, since mapping these behaviors is work no one can do alone.

talks.title: How I Used and Abused LLMs to Get Top 250 on HTB
talks.teaser: Walks through building a semiautonomous LLM workflow with jailbreaks, tool access and memory to solve Hack The Box machines.
talks.summary:
The talk documents an experiment in giving AI assistants broad access to a personal machine so they could work through Hack The Box, a platform of deliberately vulnerable machines scored by user and root flags. The speaker describes the setup as a semiautonomous workflow rather than a single chat, combining shell access, a notes store, a browser, graph-based memory, and jailbroken model access that could fall back between providers, including a local model.

Progress was tracked in stages, with each stage rated by how much of a machine the assistant completed on its own. Early versions helped only modestly, around 10 to 15 percent, before reaching roughly 70 and then 90 percent. The high point was undercut when firewall logs revealed the assistant had reached a published writeup for a machine, which prompted a rework: the persona shifted toward learning rather than handing over answers, and each working directory loaded its own prompt and pinned tools. Later versions saved attack-path notes as scripts that restored a checkpoint on a box, and the assistant could fetch and compile public exploits.

The speaker concludes that the setup was strongest at repetitive setup, scanning, Active Directory steps and coding challenges, while the human still chose the approach and open-ended targets without known CVEs were not really tested. Practical lessons included managing context window limits with structured memory instead of large prompts, pinning tool versions, and keeping logs. The speaker sees the same ideas extending to penetration testing and bug bounty work, and warns against running such agents near real data.

talks.title: Planning a Project That Has No Budget
talks.teaser: Offers practical ways for solo developers and volunteer teams to plan work when no budget or deadline sets a finish line.
talks.summary:
Travis Southard opens by noting that many software projects have a finish line set by a client's budget or grant, while volunteer and internal projects often have none. Without a payer saying "stop," it is hard to tell when a project is done or when requests have become excessive. He frames his advice around his work as a nonprofit legal aid developer and as a volunteer project lead, and says the views are his own rather than those of his employer.

The middle of the talk covers what tends to go wrong and what helps. Waiting until the last minute to start each task, which he calls just-in-time delivery, creates a fragile cycle where one slip pushes back everything after it. He suggests learning your team's real pace, padding estimates substantially, writing down steps and a clear definition of done, and keeping deadlines on a separate calendar. Urgency should be judged by who is blocked and how much harm a delay causes. He recommends building a rough working version before polishing, reusing templates and existing tools where possible, and keeping setup documentation current so newcomers can work independently.

He closes by arguing that planning is continuous rather than a one-time step at the start. Regular check-ins, honest timelines with stakeholders, and deliberate choices about design keep a project sustainable. Audience questions covered burnout on long-running projects, gathering feedback from users, and how to decline requests. His answers included cutting scope to a bare minimum, taking a break, and deferring a request to a later date when there is capacity.

talks.title: The Struggle for Connection in a Fragmented World: Rebuilding Third Spaces
talks.teaser: Traces the decline of hacker third spaces and suggests practical ways to rebuild in-person community.
talks.summary:
Jack Gangi argues that third spaces, the informal gathering places between home and work such as cafes, libraries, local shops and game stores, are disappearing, and that hacker culture has long relied on them. He traces the decline through suburban development, thin retail margins, online shopping, and the gentrification cycle that pushes out small businesses and longtime residents. He also notes how chain stores and rising rents make neighborhoods less welcoming over time.

The talk then turns to the forces that have weakened connection more recently. Remote work blurs the line between home and job, gig work fragments daily schedules, and online platforms can remove communities at will. Gangi points to shadow banning, engagement-driven algorithms that amplify provocative content, and the health effects of loneliness. He argues that the informal learning and mentorship found in shared spaces, where people pick up unexpected skills, are hard to replicate online.

For rebuilding, he recommends joining or starting a local hacker space, attending hackathons and 2600 meetings, volunteering, and simply showing up regularly. Audience questions covered cheap ways to rent meeting space, making groups welcoming to newcomers and women, avoiding cliquish behavior, and the difference between hacker and maker spaces. The takeaway is that in-person connection takes deliberate effort, and that small, consistent groups can keep it alive.

talks.title: Eternal Soup
talks.teaser: Experimental trio from Jersey City blends pops, vocals, trumpet and electronics into a shifting live set.

talks.title: Neon Edge
talks.teaser: Shows how a live electronic set is built and how synthesis, filters and delay effects shape its sound.
talks.summary:
Neon Edge opened with a set of original tracks played on a keyboard, DJ controller and clip launcher, with song structure chosen on the fly so each performance differs. Part of the set mashed up older songs in real time, and one piece was improvised on the spot. The performance was followed by a short session on sound design aimed at newcomers.

The session started with the difference between raw sound sources and effects, then walked through waveforms such as sine, triangle, sawtooth and square, and how stacked harmonics set a sound's brightness. A low-pass filter with resonance was shown shaping a square wave, with the cutoff tied to key pressure. To thicken a patch without the phasing that classic unison produces, random noise was applied to the pitch of each oscillator. The talk then covered how short delays with feedback can imitate a plucked string, and how many delay lines combine into reverb, with early and late reflections explained. The demo closed with pitch modulation producing metallic tones, shown on a spectrogram.

The main takeaway was to trust your ear over the meters when adjusting controls, and to treat delay and reverb as building blocks for both rhythm and space.

talks.title: A History of Music: From Handel to House
talks.teaser: Plays a thirty-minute piano medley tracing music from 1729 to 2025, with live improvisation based on audience suggestions.
talks.summary:
Randy Naraine opens a late-night piano set at the conference by recalling his first visit to the event years ago, before he worked in security. He explains the format: one continuous medley that moves from Baroque and Romantic classical pieces through ragtime, early jazz, blues, the standards of the 1950s, and the top songs of each following decade, ending with recent music from 2025. The setlist is shared through a QR code, and a MIDI visualizer behind him shows the notes, dynamics and melody as he plays.

Between pieces he talks about his years as a music teacher and his belief that students can write their own music instead of only following the printed page. He invites audience members to describe a memory, a feeling or a sound, then improvises short pieces around those suggestions. One of these is a gospel-inspired improvisation built from a listener's description, and he also reminisces about the old hotel that hosted the conference in earlier years.

The set closes with thanks, an offer to send the recorded MIDI file to anyone who emails him, and an encore request for a slower, lower-octave version of one piece. The talk has no security content. It shows how a MIDI controller can turn a live performance into generative visual art, and how improvisation can be approached by anyone willing to experiment.
